articles.title: Nvidia shares up nearly 33% and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
articles.summary: The jump in Nvidia shares has also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq up 7%.
articles.content:
Nvidia shares skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.

Nvidia shares had risen by nearly 33% by midday ET (17:00 GMT), boosting its market value by about $1 trillion and also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq up by nearly 7%.

Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday , with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.

Live updates: Jensen Huang returns as CEO following affair with alleged spy

Amazon shares were up by nearly 4% and Microsoft shares were up nearly 3%, while other major tech firms including Apple saw more modest gains, up less than 2%.

Other chipmakers also experienced large increases. Micron Technology jumped 19%, and Intel shares climbed nearly 13%.

While the surge in Nvidia shares was large, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.

A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.

Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".

"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.

"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.

"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.

"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

articles.title: Child safety groups urge Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys until proved safe
articles.summary: Advocates from across the world voice concern over privacy issues and inappropriate communication to children More than 150 child safety groups and experts across six continents have urged Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys this Christmas until they are proved to be safe. In a letter sent to Amazon’s president, Andy Jassy, and eBay’s president, Jamie Iannone, the coalition called for the online retailers to stop the sale of AI toys and offer refunds to customers who have already bought one. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Advocates from across the world voice concern over privacy issues and inappropriate communication to children

More than 150 child safety groups and experts across six continents have urged Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys this Christmas until they are proved to be safe.

In a letter sent to Amazon’s president, Andy Jassy, and eBay’s president, Jamie Iannone, the coalition called for the online retailers to stop the sale of AI toys and offer refunds to customers who have already bought one.

The coalition, which includes the psychologist Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation Movement and UK and US child safety groups, says the risks associated with these toys are “well documented”.

One plush bunny was listed for ages three and older while being connected to ChatGPT, whose own terms require users to be 13 or older. When tested by the UK group Alliance 4 Children , the toy suggested a child could give consent to being touched for pleasure.

The listing was pulled by Amazon, but after 48 hours the toy returned to the platform under a new retailer, according to Alliance 4 Children. The second listing has now been removed by Amazon.

“These toys are cheap, easy to buy and largely untested,” the letter stated, also noting that they were marketed towards children as young as three years old.

The letter states that nearly 30 AI-enabled toys were available on Amazon’s UK website in late October, while about 50 were recently found on sale on Amazon in the US.

Several toys were advertised as being able to clone family members’ voices and provide “emotional growth tracking” for children.

In March 2026, a study by the University of Cambridge for the Childhood Trust found that young children were forming emotional bonds with AI toys. It also found no evidence on possible benefits to children’s development.

“The precautionary principle applies,” the letter said. “These products should be shown to be safe before they reach children, not withdrawn one at a time after harm is found.”

Last Tuesday, the United States Public Interest Research Group published a report after testing seven AI toys. It found that most of the products reviewed were still too faulty to be on the market, and had big privacy issues or responded inappropriately to questions from children. One toy was found to unexpectedly take photos of the testers.

On Friday, a letter signed by 52 MPs and peers was handed in at No 10, calling for the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, to restrict the sale of AI toys until they have been proved safe.

The letter also asks for the Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) to issue an alert for parents and retailers about the risks of buying AI toys before Christmas.

Signatories include the MPs Jess Asato, Sharon Hodgson, Andrea Leadsom and Caroline Dinenage.

“AI chatbot toys are not safe for children – it is as simple as that,” said Asato. “Parents expect that toys they buy for their kids are safe; they don’t expect those toys to give sexual responses or advocate suicide.

“In the run-up to Christmas, it is imperative that the government acts to make retailers and parents aware of the very real risks and work to prohibit the sale of these toys.”

The government launched a review into its toy safety regulation in July, including the emerging risks posed by AI-enabled toys. Calls for evidence closed on 6 October.

A spokesperson for Amazon said: “ We require all products sold by third-party sellers in our store to comply with applicable laws and regulations. Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families.

“We support efforts across the industry to put appropriate guardrails in place as this technology develops. We’ve removed the named products in question as we review claims.”

A spokesperson for eBay said: “We are committed to protecting buyers and sellers on our marketplace. We continually evaluate our policies, engage with regulators, and comply with applicable laws to help ensure our marketplace remains safe, trusted, and responsive to evolving safety standards.”

A spokesperson for the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said: “We are very concerned by these reports and are already investigating these products, as well as the potential risks posed by AI in toys.

“There is no excuse for anyone to sell products that could put children at risk, and companies need to do all they can to act quickly and put things right.”

articles.title: How freaked out should we be? After mass outages, experts tell us how close we are to ‘doomsday’
articles.summary: As tech, travel and banking failures sweep the US, analysts and cyber-security directors discuss AI, underfunding and what keeps them up at night Grounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly. Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure. Continue reading...
articles.content:
As tech, travel and banking failures sweep the US, analysts and cyber-security directors discuss AI, underfunding and what keeps them up at night

G rounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly.

Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure.

For their part, politicians and the spokespeople of affected companies a have denied such master plots. And while many presumed that the nationwide airline ground stoppage on 13 November resulted from the Federal Aviation Administration’s rollout of new AI-assisted administration software (called, perhaps aspirationally, the Smart System), the FAA themselves laid the blame on a downed router in Arkansas . Microsoft has chalked the recent outage to Outlook not to malicious intrusions, but some buggy code that has been laying dormant for months. Some people will buy such explanations. Others, naturally, may remain skeptical.

Just how worried should we be? Are these disruptions just a new, extremely annoying part of daily life?

The Guardian spoke to experts across fields to understand how AI and other threats are jeopardizing critical infrastructure, and how exactly we’re mitigating worst-case scenarios.

Did the FAA’s nationwide ground stoppage in November surprise you at all?

The extent of this outage was surprising. And to be honest, the excuses about what caused it are not credible. The FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure is fully duplicated, fully redundant; every link, every node. There are tens of thousands of nodes and pieces of hardware. The idea that one router in Arkansas could take down an entire network is not credible.

Can you give me a sense of how in need of upgrades the FAA’s systems are?

Well, they’re held together with rubber bands and chewing gum and paperclips. But paperclips are conducting! They’re actually good conductors! But they’re 50-year-old systems. A lot of the basic architecture is old, and analog, and it’s being replaced over time.

There was some speculation that the outage had to do with the FAA rolling out this new AI-system, the S mart System. Do you give any credence to that?

That happens to be my theory on the outage. I work in this area, and we have deployed what you can call “AI” if you want, but I would call computer-based operations research techniques. But it’s designed to reduce airspace congestion and complexity. This Smart System has some AI, which is to say it involves computers talking to pilots. It’s designed to help flight-tracking, and reduce delays and it’s been tested on a carrier-level, with individual airlines. There’s been no issues. What happened, I believe, was that the FAA tried to roll it out simultaneously, for all flights across the nation, which has a bigger risk.

The network gets overwhelmed with these administrative messages, saying, basically, “instead of flying this trajectory, fly an alternate trajectory.” If you have a large number of these messages, it will cause quality problems with radar data, radio data and, to some degree, voice data. When you overwhelm the network with administrative crap, you can cause the quality of radar data to deteriorate. That’s when people working air-traffic control get understandably concerned. And they respond to that by cutting the volume in the system, and just shutting it down.

What are the things you are worried about, as the airlines and FAA try to modernize their infrastructure?

It’s understandable that we want everything to be up to date. Since I’ve been looking at this problem, we’ve spent close to $150bn over four generations of system upgrades. And we basically have the same system. And it doesn’t address the issue of delays. It’s an own goal. They’re not using their institutional knowledge of what is the likely outcome, and not testing it adequately. They tested it on 180 flights over 60 days, in Washington, and then said: “We’re good to go. We’re just going to do all nationwide fights.”

So the worst-case scenario is people implementing things at scale, without adequate testing, and understanding what could happen. You can overwhelm that telecommunications infrastructure. Don’t be concerned about flight safety. Pilots, and their dispatchers, and FAA, they’re professionals. They ensure the system is safe. That’s what gets us to a vanishingly low accident rate.

In your view, what motivation does the FAA have to cover up the cause of the outage?

They don’t have much invested in a single router. But they do have a lot of investment in their new AI system. And I’m not alone in thinking this. A lot of air traffic controllers have been speaking out about it. They don’t buy the router theory either.

William Wetherill : chief information security officer at Defense Storm, a cyber-attack risk management agency servicing banks, credit unions and financial institutions

A recent report on the state of the banking industry showed that 81% of financial institutions surveyed reported unauthori zed access and other cyber-security intrusions in the past year. That seems like a lot.

The amount of attacks that you see is kind of incredible. Banks have always been juicy targets for attacks. And that doesn’t change today. AI has made attacks cheaper. When you’re in this world, and see what’s happening, well, everyone is getting attacked all the time.

If they could just steal money, they’d do it. But that money is all insured. And it’s traceable. The FBI can track them down in 24 hours. Sometimes they’ll try moving money: hack a business email and get into the middle of the transaction and change the routing number. But it’s usually more about extortion. They’ll steal data from banks and credit unions, which we call “target rich”. Then they threaten to release it, unless they’re paid however many million dollars. It’s more about the ransom. They’re looking for the institutions to pay crypto, so it’s not traceable. The damage you can do is pretty high. You could shut down a credit union, if they get ransomed too much and consumers lose confidence.

What is the closest a financial institution has come to a total breakdown?

What we just witnessed with multiple banks going down was a major event. For those of us whose money is stored in online bank accounts, and whose livelihoods are stored by credit unions, we don’t have access to our funds, that’s about as critical as you can get. That’s devastating, on a smaller scale.

The biggest thing that can happen is attacking our backbone: infrastructure like Swift payments that are the underlying fabric of financial transactions across the globe. If those come down, that would be our doomsday. But that hasn’t happened, yet.

The majority of cybercrime is financially motivated. [Financial criminals] don’t have the motivation to kill the one thing that’s helping them. You destroy banking, you destroy this technology, and you destroy the entire world.

The first thing to understand, and I’ll say this loud and clear, is that nothing has fundamentally changed. The speed and breadth of attacks has changed. But it’s all things we’ve already dealt with. There’s a lot of paranoia. And people really, really suffer for it. When you have your identity stolen, it’s really exposing, and mental health comes into play. You have to understand that these are blanket attacks, you’re not being targeted, personally. When I deal with individuals, I want them to understand that in this case, you aren’t special. And that should make you feel better. An individual shouldn’t have a mindset where they’re prepping for the end of the world constantly.

Dr Scott J White : director of the cyber-security program and cyber academy at George Washington University, former officer with the Canadian Security Intelligence Service

Anyone with a laptop computer and connectivity can now be an asymmetrical threat against the west. A lot of minor actors, who never had the capability, now AI makes them active players. AI is a threat multiplier. Who are these threat actors?

We have what we call our advanced persistent threats, or APTs. There are four major ones: China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. But every time America moves in the world, we’re going to get a proxy. For example, with the American incursion into Venezuela, you’re going to see people who support Venezuela, or Venezuelans, start to attack the United States. As the US continues its conflict with Iran, we have Iranian proxies globally that will be launching attacks against us globally. Now you’re adding a very low-level, low-skilled individual with AI, and we have to start using AI as a defensive structure as well. We’re asking AI to try and find these threat vectors, as they’re coming in. It doesn’t surprise me at all that these attacks are coming in. You have to remember that every new piece of software that comes out, our adversaries are also getting that same piece of software. They’re reverse-engineering it.

In the event that these defen ses aren’t sufficient, or aren’t implemented swiftly enough, what’s the worst thing that can happen?

The worst case-scenario, globally, would be incursions into water treatment facilities, hospitals, and so on. Imagine launching a cyber-attack against a country: take its communication, and water treatment facilities, and energy distribution nodes offline. Make the country blind. Then follow with a kinetic attack. How successful would that be? It would be extremely successful. Leave the country blind, and unarmed. Then follow with a traditional attack. That’s a formula for success.

The probability of such a scenario remains relatively low. The Russians are well aware that an attack of this nature could trigger a rapid and significant escalation, potentially extending to the use of nuclear weapons. The consequences would be extraordinarily severe and the risks of triggering a broader global conflict would be difficult for any party to control or predict. That said, a low probability does not mean the scenario can be dismissed or overlooked.

It seems like cyber -security can only play catch up to advanced attacks from AI hackers.

Absolutely we’re playing catchup. That’s exactly the problem. We have something called “security by design”, sometimes called the “zero trust” security approach. This is when you build out a system from the beginning, accounting for threat vectors. But not all systems are built like this. And it’s very difficult to retrofit those kinds of systems. We continue to layer security and try to create a smaller attack surface and limit the attacker, and how they can get to us. That’s the world we are in. Is it a dystopian world? I wouldn’t go that far. But it’s going to require us to do a lot more upgrading on our security. These responses have been condensed and edited for clarity

The amount of attacks that you see is kind of incredible. Banks have always been juicy targets for attacks. And that doesn’t change today. AI has made attacks cheaper. When you’re in this world, and see what’s happening, well, everyone is getting attacked all the time.

If they could just steal money, they’d do it. But that money is all insured. And it’s traceable. The FBI can track them down in 24 hours. Sometimes they’ll try moving money: hack a business email and get into the middle of the transaction and change the routing number. But it’s usually more about extortion. They’ll steal data from banks and credit unions, which we call “target rich”. Then they threaten to release it, unless they’re paid however many million dollars. It’s more about the ransom. They’re looking for the institutions to pay crypto, so it’s not traceable. The damage you can do is pretty high. You could shut down a credit union, if they get ransomed too much and consumers lose confidence.
What is the closest a financial institution has come to a total breakdown?

What we just witnessed with multiple banks going down was a major event. For those of us whose money is stored in online bank accounts, and whose livelihoods are stored by credit unions, we don’t have access to our funds, that’s about as critical as you can get. That’s devastating, on a smaller scale.

The biggest thing that can happen is attacking our backbone: infrastructure like Swift payments that are the underlying fabric of financial transactions across the globe. If those come down, that would be our doomsday. But that hasn’t happened, yet.

The majority of cybercrime is financially motivated. [Financial criminals] don’t have the motivation to kill the one thing that’s helping them. You destroy banking, you destroy this technology, and you destroy the entire world.

The first thing to understand, and I’ll say this loud and clear, is that nothing has fundamentally changed. The speed and breadth of attacks has changed. But it’s all things we’ve already dealt with. There’s a lot of paranoia. And people really, really suffer for it. When you have your identity stolen, it’s really exposing, and mental health comes into play. You have to understand that these are blanket attacks, you’re not being targeted, personally. When I deal with individuals, I want them to understand that in this case, you aren’t special. And that should make you feel better. An individual shouldn’t have a mindset where they’re prepping for the end of the world constantly.
Dr Scott J White : director of the cyber-security program and cyber academy at George Washington University, former officer with the Canadian Security Intelligence Service

Anyone with a laptop computer and connectivity can now be an asymmetrical threat against the west. A lot of minor actors, who never had the capability, now AI makes them active players. AI is a threat multiplier. Who are these threat actors?

We have what we call our advanced persistent threats, or APTs. There are four major ones: China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. But every time America moves in the world, we’re going to get a proxy. For example, with the American incursion into Venezuela, you’re going to see people who support Venezuela, or Venezuelans, start to attack the United States. As the US continues its conflict with Iran, we have Iranian proxies globally that will be launching attacks against us globally. Now you’re adding a very low-level, low-skilled individual with AI, and we have to start using AI as a defensive structure as well. We’re asking AI to try and find these threat vectors, as they’re coming in. It doesn’t surprise me at all that these attacks are coming in. You have to remember that every new piece of software that comes out, our adversaries are also getting that same piece of software. They’re reverse-engineering it.
In the event that these defen ses aren’t sufficient, or aren’t implemented swiftly enough, what’s the worst thing that can happen?

The worst case-scenario, globally, would be incursions into water treatment facilities, hospitals, and so on. Imagine launching a cyber-attack against a country: take its communication, and water treatment facilities, and energy distribution nodes offline. Make the country blind. Then follow with a kinetic attack. How successful would that be? It would be extremely successful. Leave the country blind, and unarmed. Then follow with a traditional attack. That’s a formula for success.

The probability of such a scenario remains relatively low. The Russians are well aware that an attack of this nature could trigger a rapid and significant escalation, potentially extending to the use of nuclear weapons. The consequences would be extraordinarily severe and the risks of triggering a broader global conflict would be difficult for any party to control or predict. That said, a low probability does not mean the scenario can be dismissed or overlooked.
It seems like cyber -security can only play catch up to advanced attacks from AI hackers.

Absolutely we’re playing catchup. That’s exactly the problem. We have something called “security by design”, sometimes called the “zero trust” security approach. This is when you build out a system from the beginning, accounting for threat vectors. But not all systems are built like this. And it’s very difficult to retrofit those kinds of systems. We continue to layer security and try to create a smaller attack surface and limit the attacker, and how they can get to us. That’s the world we are in. Is it a dystopian world? I wouldn’t go that far. But it’s going to require us to do a lot more upgrading on our security. These responses have been condensed and edited for clarity

articles.title: Village's concern over sewage discharge in dry river
articles.summary: Campaigners call for restrictions on sewage treatment plant discharging effluent during drought
articles.content:
Alice Elliott is part of the Citizen's Science Project in Peterchurch, who want restrictions on treated discharges during drought

A group of residents have said pools of treated sewage are forming on a dry riverbed that runs through their village during drought conditions.

They are calling for the Environment Agency to stop the sewage treatment plant in Peterchurch, Herefordshire, discharging into the River Dore during periods of no flow.

At the moment, Welsh Water legally discharges directly into the river, but campaigners said its permit assumed the effluent would be diluted by the river flow.

The company said the plant was operating in accordance with the permit, but it was liaising with residents over their concerns.

Locals have formed a Citizen's Science Project for the Dore catchment and say lab tests have shown the waste contains "high levels of nitrate and phosphorus" as well as harmful bacteria including "worrying amounts of E. coli".

The River Dore that feeds into the Monnow and then the Wye, has seen long periods of 'no flow' over the last 15 years

Alice Elliott from the group said they had seen periods of drought affecting the river level for several years:

"Where the river stops flowing it goes completely dry, absolutely no flow.

"The sewage treatment works is continually discharging onto a dry riverbed and it's created a large pool of treated but undiluted effluent."

The group said it had samples from the site tested in a laboratory and were seeing "high levels of nitrate and phosphorus".

"We've noticed that it contains worrying amounts of E. coli and other bacteria that are harmful to health... Normally it would get diluted down and that's what the permit allows".

It is thought the area is surrounded by a permeable gravel bed and residents are concerned the "extensive pool" is being allowed to "permeate through the ground and through the soil around it."

The dry bed also becomes a lure for children playing during drought conditions.

"It was like a sunken road, it was an exciting environment and the children were skipping along, unaware that a few metres away is a big pool of treated sewage."

Rosie Lane collects samples from the "extensive pool" of effluent sitting on the dry river bed near the sewage treatment plant in Peterchurch

The group has demanded answers from both Welsh Water and the Environment Agency.

"What we've asked is how do they go about assessing and issuing their permits for Welsh Water? What are they doing in terms of assessing the environmental impact when they know there is a period of no flow. What action... what plans are they putting in place to combat that?" said Elliott.

The River Dore flows into the Monnow, which then joins the River Wye at Monmouth - a river that has had it's fair share of publicity over alleged contamination, leading to it becoming the first river in the UK to get its own special protection charter.

The outlet from the Welsh Water sewage treatment plant as it is released into the River Dore at Peterchurch

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "Protecting and improving water quality is a priority for the Environment Agency, and we understand the concerns raised by local residents about conditions in the River Dore during prolonged dry weather.

"Peterchurch sewage treatment works' discharge is permitted and currently understood to be compliant. We continue to monitor conditions in the River Dore."

"Peterchurch waste water treatment works is operating as it should and within the permit conditions issued by our regulator.

"The treated effluent is routinely sampled and tested and we are liaising with the Dore Citizen Science group and the Environment Agency on this matter."

Campaigners dressed as chickens take regulator to Court over poultry farm pollution fears

articles.content:
The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided

I n as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter.

Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered.

And when you’ve conceded more goals in all competitions this season than anybody else in Europe’s top five leagues, and when you’ve let in more in the league than anybody other than Crystal Palace, it’s pretty obvious that the defence is a major problem. There are serious reasons for concern; a switch of manager alone will not magically save United.

Perhaps Yoro was unfortunate to be sent off. Senne Lammens may have got to the ball ahead of Alexander Isak. But the opposite is also true. Had Yoro not been sent off, it would only have been because Isak’s first touch was heavy. By far the bigger issue as Pochettino prepares for Wednesday’s Champions League game at Sporting and Saturday’s Premier League match at home to Brentford is how easily United were undone by a simple ball over the top. First Matthijs de Ligt, who was much deeper than the rest of the defensive line, inexcusably left it, and then Yoro, in scrambling back, made an appallingly clumsy foul.

De Ligt, who has only been back in training for six weeks as he recovers from a back injury, had not started a league game since November last year. He looked way off the pace, as he had in the defeat to Como , and his selection, in retrospect, was an error by Pochettino. Yoro, who had looked one of United’s better recent signings in his first year after signing from Lille, had become a case study in the damage being part of a dysfunctional team can do to a player: his confidence is shot and he now lurches around like a sad horse, a player who seems always to be at the centre of unfortunate events – such as that header against his own bar against Aston Villa.

There are manifold problems at United, from the leadership to the recruitment to the stadium, but if there is to be an improvement in form, the first thing Pochettino needs to do is to change the mood. This is nothing like a great squad. It is a mess of ideas and strategies, put together over six different managers with no consistent goal in sight. But it is not a squad made up of terrible players. It is a squad made up of players who have lost their way, who had been dragged down into the morass. It’s obvious that United should be better than this, but even this United should be better than this.

United have won only one of 11 games in the league this season, and that was against newly-promoted Ipswich in August . To put that in context, Burnley are the only other side of all 92 in the league not to have won at least twice; when United were relegated in 1973-74 , they won three of their first 11 games. Bruno Fernades has now played in four defeats to Liverpool by four goals or more, a record.

It remains, still, almost inconceivable that United will be relegated, or even that they will find themselves in a proper battle. It’s almost a category error; this cannot happen. But there are no terrible sides in the Premier League this season. Perhaps Manchester City’s appeal will fail and their punishment means they will obligingly occupy one of the relegation slots. But the three promoted sides are all showing signs of fight. Crystal Palace will probably improve under Thomas Frank, Sunderland have started keeping clean sheets and are a very different side if Brian Brobbey is fit, Nottingham Forest are far better than their league positions suggests and Fulham are five league games unbeaten.

A bounce will, surely, come at some point under Pochettino but, this season, nothing can be taken for granted at the bottom.

articles.title: Nations Championship finals weekend to kick off in front of 40,000 empty seats
articles.summary: Organisers to close top tier of Allianz Stadium on Friday Saturday and Sunday sales stronger with 70% taken The opening night of the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend on Friday is poised to be played in front of around 40,000 empty seats, with the top tier of the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham to be closed. The Guardian has learned that more than 50% of tickets at the 82,000-capacity venue for the Ireland v Australia/Italy v Fiji double-header remained available on Monday. That figure could grow after tournament organisers opened a ticket swap exchange for fans wanting to watch their team. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The opening night of the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend on Friday is poised to be played in front of around 40,000 empty seats, with the top tier of the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham to be closed.

The Guardian has learned that more than 50% of tickets at the 82,000-capacity venue for the Ireland v Australia/Italy v Fiji double-header remained available on Monday. That figure could grow after tournament organisers opened a ticket swap exchange for fans wanting to watch their team.

Ticket sales for Saturday and Sunday are stronger, at 70% of capacity, with Nations Championship officials hoping to sell out Saturday’s England v New Zealand/Wales v Japan double-header and Sunday, when France and South Africa will contest the final after Scotland play Argentina.

Supporters had to wait for the final round of group games to be completed on Saturday to learn which of the six fixture slots each country would play in.

Selling out three successive rugby events was always likely to be challenging, particularly the Friday, with Fiji v Italy kicking off the opening match at 4.40pm GMT.

Tickets have been competitively priced, starting at £60 (£20 for juniors) for Friday, rising to £100 on Saturday (£50 for juniors) and £125 for Sunday (£50 for juniors).

Despite the difficulties of selling tickets at the last minute the Nations Championship is committed to the finals weekend concept, although Qatar have pulled out of hosting in 2028 due to the Middle East conflict, as the Guardian revealed earlier this month.

TV viewing figures have been far more positive, with ITV averaging audiences of 3m across all fixtures and Wales’ shock win over New Zealand gaining more than 4m.

The organisers of the Nations Championship, the Six Nations and Sanzaar, declined to comment on ticket sales for the final weekend.

articles.content:
From Rubbermaid to Glasslock, we tested every kind of storage container. These silicone covers, glass jars and vacuum sealers deserve a spot in your kitchen

‘The perfect food storage finally exists’: I tried the new Anydeli plastic-free containers

Welcome to Filter finds , a series where Filter contributors share the things they love most – and think you might, too.

Thanksgiving is just around the corner … which means your fridge may soon be overflowing with leftover turkey, stuffing and more mashed potatoes than you know what to do with. Before the feast (and game of Tetris in the fridge), it is worth getting your food storage situation in order. We asked our contributors to share their favorite containers and clever storage solutions , from freezer-friendly glassware to stretchy lids to metal snack bowls.

I recently transitioned all of my daughter’s bento boxes and food storage to stainless steel pieces from Lalo, and I couldn’t be happier with the change. These nesting bowls are dishwasher friendly and take up minimal space in my small kitchen, and I don’t have to worry about any chemicals leeching into her leftovers. Plus, the colors are so cheerful – no sad beige Tupperware here. Oset Babür-Winter

What delights me about these storage containers is that I don’t know how I got them: maybe they arrived as part of a shipment of hot soup from my mom when I was sick, or maybe they’re a result of my aunts’ tendency to send me home with a week’s worth of leftovers during the holidays. My slow accumulation of the full collection over the years has been a blessing for my own storage needs. They’re completely leakproof, they behave in the microwave, freezer, dishwasher and oven (without lids), and they preserve the taste of food even when it feels as though I’m pushing their best-before date. Marissa Miller

I was once the type to tote around snacks in a single-use Ziploc bag, or worse, a wilted tissue. I have now seen the light after discovering these “bento boxes” for mess-free snack storage. Their six half-cup compartments give me plenty of variety to fuel up on, and each compartment features its own snap-on lid, limiting mess for when I’m, say, eating in a moving car. Yes, the aesthetic is a little juvenile, but I’ll take anything that’ll get my two-year-old to eat her fruits and vegetables. Marissa Miller

Our vacuum sealer helps make the most of homemade meals, bulk purchases and fresh produce. As vegans living in a small town, there aren’t many options for eating out, so batching cuts the amount of time spent in the kitchen. We just cook more than needed for a meal, then portion and vacuum seal the leftovers for the freezer. On busy days, it’s nice to know lunch won’t take long.

A vacuum sealer is particularly handy for bulk purchases such as our 12lb boxes of Butler soy curls or Om Noms protein curls, which arrive in enormous bags. And as winter approaches, we’ll be using it to freeze seasonal produce from local farmers’ markets and our farm share. Alan Truly

I have used this brand’s containers for 20 years. I especially like the secure, snap-on lids, which have four locking tabs and a leak-proof rubber seal.

But what I enjoy most is the versatility: with the lid off, Glasslock can go from freezer to microwave or oven, then straight to the table on a trivet. It’s a great way to reheat and serve lasagna or enchiladas (or any holiday leftover), plus the variety of sizes works for nearly any dish, from sauces to complete meals. If you get a set, the containers stack neatly in the fridge. They are heavier than plastic, but that’s a fair trade for sturdy, reusable dishes that handle almost every stage of meal prep. Alan Truly

We like getting food in bulk because it saves us money and keeps us stocked up for future winter storms. But storing a giant bag of flour, oats or beans can be a challenge. We don’t want to vacuum seal everything, and that is where screw-on bucket lids help.

These lids turn ordinary five-gallon buckets into airtight storage containers. The outer ring can be a bit challenging to push into place, but once the ring is sealed, I can open and close the bucket with a twist, sealing dry goods to keep them fresher. The sealed buckets protect food from pests and moisture, and they are sturdy enough to keep in a spare room instead of overloading kitchen cupboards. And, when unexpected company arrives, we can even add a cushion to make a sealed bucket into an impromptu stool, or a tray to make it into a side table. Alan Truly

We love a good cheese and charcuterie board in this household, so when it comes to entertaining , I tend to go a bit overboard with the spread. If you ever find yourself “burdened” with leftover wedges and slabs of cheese, deli meat slices or a mix of both, it can be hard to store everything properly.

Enter these trays by Crudités – they have a unique lid made of stretchable plastic. The concave lid and plastic hold food snugly in place, so you can essentially assemble a mini cheese platter and pop it into the fridge to snack on later. If you flip the lid over, you have more vertical space that accommodates bigger chunks of cheese or larger dishes such as an artfully arranged salad. It’s a genius design, and I am glad I no longer have to waste a bunch of disposable sandwich bags or plastic wrap to store extra charcuterie. Bernadette Machard de Gramont

My husband runs a restaurant kitchen as its head chef, so naturally, the food storage he uses on the line trickles its way into our cupboards. These quart-sized square containers are a busy kitchen staple because they stack seamlessly to save space and they’re microwavable and dishwasher-safe. Neither too compact nor too bulky, they have become the default food storage vessel in our home, whether we’re freezing leftovers after a weeknight or holiday feast or stashing our mise en place before firing up the stove. Marissa Miller

According to the USDA , it is perfectly safe to store food in the container from whence they came for up to four days. And according to another authority – my dog, who gets wet food mixed with kibble every night – they taste plenty good. For a long time, we covered his leftover food with a small plate (precarious) or plastic wrap (wasteful and finicky). Then I discovered this silicone cover, which has three concentric rings on the underside that form a tight seal on cans of (nearly) all sizes. It’s marketed for cat food, but it fits our dog’s 13.2oz cans of food perfectly. In fact, with the exception of a big 28oz can of tomatoes, the cover fits every can in our pantry. Juno DeMelo

Something about the aesthetics of these jars elevates everything you put in them. I love using the small sizes for vinaigrettes, larger ones for stocks, sauces and leftovers, and the tall cylinders for homemade pickles. Pro tips: the pretty deco and tulip shapes are great for edible gifts – especially with wood lids . And if you want jars you can stick in the freezer, buy the mold or quadro shape, since any brand of jars with curved sides or sloped “shoulders” that narrow at the top can get damaged as the contents freeze and expand. Elizabeth Brownfield

I run an online culinary school, and earlier this year my book on preserving food was published, so proper food storage is often front of mind. My forever pick is a classic for a reason: pint-sized mason jars. I like these Ball wide-mouth jars because they’re easy to fill, but really, any mason jar has a place in my heart. Use them for storing dry goods or for leftovers, sauces and more – and of course, for canning. Julia Skinner

articles.title: David Raya’s shoulder injury ‘not too serious’ and no surgery needed for Arsenal goalkeeper
articles.summary: No 1 to miss Dortmund game but could return for City clash ‘We were worried … he’s better than expected,’ says manager Mikel Arteta is hopeful the ­shoulder injury David Raya sustained at Newcastle is not too serious, but confirmed the goalkeeper would miss Tuesday’s Champions League game against Borussia Dortmund. Raya was forced off in the ­second half of Saturday’s 2-2 draw with a ­suspected dislocated shoulder, ­raising fears he could be sidelined for an extended period. He had an MRI scan on Arsenal’s return to London and was absent from ­training on Monday. Kepa Arrizabalaga is expected to deputise at home to Dortmund. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Mikel Arteta is hopeful the ­shoulder injury David Raya sustained at Newcastle is not too serious, but confirmed the goalkeeper would miss Tuesday’s Champions League game against Borussia Dortmund.

Raya was forced off in the ­second half of Saturday’s 2-2 draw with a ­suspected dislocated shoulder, ­raising fears he could be sidelined for an extended period. He had an MRI scan on Arsenal’s return to London and was absent from ­training on Monday. Kepa Arrizabalaga is expected to deputise at home to Dortmund.

“He’s not fit for tomorrow, ­unfortunately, but it doesn’t look too serious,” the manager said. “With the pain he was showing immediately after the action we were all quite ­worried, but he seems to be better than what we expected. There’s no need of surgery, which was the main fear.”

Asked whether Raya could play at home to Manchester City on ­Sunday, Arteta said: “Tomorrow we’ll have more tests and we will know. I think we’ve seen what David brings to the team. That’s why we are very ­protective with Kepa and [third-choice] Illan [Meslier]. Everybody needs to be ready because these things happen.”

Dortmund are a point behind Arsenal in the Champions League after three wins from their first four matches and Niko Kovac’s side lead Bayern Munich by two points at the top of the Bundesliga. Arteta said a youthful side expected to feature Jobe Bellingham – who was called up by England for the first time for the most recent international break alongside his brother, Jude – would provide a real test.

“You have to congratulate mum and dad for what they’ve done,” Arteta said of the Bellingham ­brothers. “Two amazing ­footballers, what they’re doing is ­remarkable. So let’s give credit as well to the parents.”

articles.title: ‘Celebrate, inspire, unite’: UK confirmed as host of 2035 Women’s World Cup
articles.summary: Country’s first World Cup since men’s 1966 edition in England Bid lists 22 stadiums as potential venues The UK is to host the 2035 Women’s World Cup, Fifa has confirmed. England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will stage the first World Cup hosted in the country since the 1966 men’s tournament in England. The UK bid was the only one under consideration for 2035. The 2031 tournament has been awarded, also uncontested, to the United States, Mexico, ⁠Costa Rica and Jamaica . The decisions were formalised at a virtual meeting of Fifa’s national associations on Monday. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The UK is to host the 2035 Women’s World Cup, Fifa has confirmed. England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will stage the first World Cup hosted in the country since the 1966 men’s tournament in England.

The UK bid was the only one under consideration for 2035. The 2031 tournament has been awarded, also uncontested, to the United States, Mexico, ⁠Costa Rica and Jamaica . The decisions were formalised at a virtual meeting of Fifa’s national associations on Monday.

Debbie Hewitt, the Football Association chair, said of the 2035 World Cup: “Together we will celebrate the power of women’s football, inspire the next generation and unite fans from every corner of the world.”

The UK bid lists 22 stadiums as potential venues. Sixteen are in England, three in Wales, two in Scotland and one is in Northern Ireland. Fifteen host cities are in the running (the bid officially lists 16, counting Trafford as distinct from Manchester).

Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring “visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country”. The prime minister also pointed to the sporting impact, saying it would “bring more people into the game and leave a legacy that lasts long after the final whistle”.

Wembley has been proposed for the final, having hosted it at the 2022 Women’s European Championship. Fifa has evaluated 19 stadiums, assessing them as being of “high quality”. All were awarded an score of at least four out of five, except for Elland Road in Leeds (3.9), Easter Road in Edinburgh, Windsor Park in Belfast and Nottingham’s City Ground (all 3.6). Old Trafford has been assessed by Fifa but the proposed new Manchester United stadium could play a significant role instead if built in time.

The three listed stadiums not assessed by Fifa are Birmingham City’s proposed 62,000-seat Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham’s stadium – which is due two stages of redevelopment – and Chelsea’s stadium because only a redeveloped Stamford Bridge or a new club stadium would come into the picture.

The 22 stadiums will be whittled down to between 14 and 16. The tournament is scheduled to involve 104 matches played by 48 teams over 39 days. The dates are yet to be confirmed but indicative dates of 21 June to 29 July have been informally used as a template during the bidding process.

London Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, any new Chelsea stadium or a redeveloped Stamford Bridge if it meets Fifa requirements

Manchester Etihad Stadium, Old Trafford or proposed new Manchester United stadium

The tournament is due to be the second Women’s World Cup to include 48 teams, after 2031’s event, mirroring this year’s men’s tournament and making it the largest single-sport event staged in the UK. There are to be 12 groups of four teams followed by knockouts starting with a last 32.

As revealed by the Guardian last week, Fifa is at loggerheads with the UK’s government and four football associations over the world governing body’s demands for tax-free status and exemptions from exchange-rate fees at the tournament.

England, Scotland and Wales are also due to co-host – along with the Republic of Ireland – the men’s European Championship in 2028.

articles.title: Chemicals, Covid and cabbage: why 2026 has been an amazing year for documentaries
articles.summary: With Musk, NAZA and You Can See Everything finding large audiences, non-fiction cinema is poised to break through. But there are plenty more gripping stories waiting for their turn in the spotlight There comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. The forecast is bracing, stormy, and occasionally chilling. Hours of darkness; no stars. We might not wish to live in the world IDFA shows us, but unfortunately we do, and so it pays to stay informed, be engaged. This year’s lineup of 250-plus documentaries steers us around the geopolitical hot spots, from tales of forced displacement in the West Bank to the rolling hell of Gaza; from a jungle-based guerrilla army in Myanmar (in White Tiger Column, the event’s opening night film) through to the traumatised children of the Vietnamese boat people (Carol Nguyen’s superb Still Night, Burning House). Some of these films could have been torn from the headlines. Others, like Raluca Lupascu’s gripping kitchen-sink tragedy A Modern Roma Fairytale, contain stories previously tucked away out of sight, just waiting to be told. Continue reading...

With Musk, NAZA and You Can See Everything finding large audiences, non-fiction cinema is poised to break through. But there are plenty more gripping stories waiting for their turn in the spotlight

T here comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. The forecast is bracing, stormy, and occasionally chilling. Hours of darkness; no stars.

We might not wish to live in the world IDFA shows us, but unfortunately we do, and so it pays to stay informed, be engaged. This year’s lineup of 250-plus documentaries steers us around the geopolitical hot spots, from tales of forced displacement in the West Bank to the rolling hell of Gaza; from a jungle-based guerrilla army in Myanmar (in White Tiger Column, the event’s opening night film) through to the traumatised children of the Vietnamese boat people (Carol Nguyen’s superb Still Night, Burning House). Some of these films could have been torn from the headlines. Others, like Raluca Lupascu’s gripping kitchen-sink tragedy A Modern Roma Fairytale, contain stories previously tucked away out of sight, just waiting to be told.

Blame the planet, says Isabel Arrate Fernandez, IDFA’s artistic director. The film-makers are responding to the world they have witnessed. “I know there’s the idea that the films will all be too depressing,” she says. “Yes, sometimes documentaries can take you to places of suffering and pain. But that’s all around us. If we turn away from that we’re only staying in our privileged bubble. And documentary cinema is so much more than just depressing and gruelling. Sometimes a film can enter your heart. And sometimes, yes, it can hit you in the stomach.”

Documentary is traditionally seen as the industry’s poor cousin, although that wealth gap may now be closing. IDFA’s 39th edition lands at the end of a breakout season for the genre, spearheaded by the success of Alex Gibney’s four-hour-long Musk , the Guardian-produced NAZA and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything , which has just passed $100m at the global box office. All three films are on the bill at IDFA. A panel discussion with the makers of NAZA lands as a last-minute addition to the programme. “It’s been tough for documentaries since the pandemic,” says Fionnuala Jamison, the managing director of NAZA’s sales agent, mk2. “This is the first year you’ve seen documentaries outside the music sphere that have broken through. So it absolutely gives us hope that things might be changing.”

Arrate Fernandez agrees it’s been a vintage year. All the same, she is keen to inject a note of caution. “It’s the buzz around a few titles that is generating this wider idea about [the success of] documentaries,” she explains. “Everyone is saying the same thing, but does that mean it is real? It’s difficult to say. At IDFA we have films from all over the world. If you fix on a few specific films – I’m thinking mainly of You Can See Everything and Musk, not so much NAZA – then there is a danger of leaving out other parts of the world.”

On balance, it is good. It means renewed interest; bums on seats. “What’s interesting for me about films like Musk or You Can See Everything is not so much that they’re breaking the rules of documentary cinema as that they are breaking the expectations and assumptions of what a documentary can achieve and the people it can reach. That’s how they’re breaking the mould and that’s what’s valuable to me. These films show that the gatekeepers have been underestimating the audience.”

I’m not sure there’s a direct line from Fielder and Oppenheim’s showstopper to the other, more obscure films on the schedule. But if it cracks open a door, that may just be enough. Beyond the big marquee screenings lies a wild, free-range bazaar where you can only pick a screening and take a punt. The Year of the Ghost, by Amsterdam-based director Louis HotHotHot, turns out to be a mordant, moving family portrait, prompted by his father’s death from Covid in China and spotlighting the disarrayed states of his widowed mother and resentful sister. Gabriel Tejedor’s excellent The Big Boom! is much larger and louder, about a dysfunctional Bulgarian town called Kazanlak, which is nourished and sustained by a nearby munitions plant. The arms manufacturer funds the annual rose festival and accompanying firework display, but it also tests explosives in the local fields and is accused of poisoning its employees with a range of hazardous chemicals. The residents largely support Russia and despise the EU. But they are also happy to make bombs that will now be shipped to Ukraine. “Thanks to this war we live really well,” they explain.

Ukraine inevitably takes the lead in numerous other films here. Hold Your Breath trails a bunch of shattered soldiers in a brief time-out from the frontline. Women and War tracks the PTSD therapy sessions of a quartet of female patients at a remote mountain retreat. Director Ruslan Fedotov, meanwhile, approaches the subject from a distance in Down the River, tracing the Dnieper’s course out of Russia and through Belarus. It moves at a leisurely pace through a world of sleepy rustic weirdness, but the military drumbeat grows more insistent the closer we get to Ukraine, because now there are battle re-enactments and conscription parades, kids perform patriotic songs inside the village hall. Fedotov’s downstream tour ends not at the sea but at a vast cemetery full of gleaming new headstones and freshly laundered Russian flags.

A river also looms large in Weicheng Hua’s extraordinary Waves of Time, which follows the final voyage of the Royal Splendor, a corroded old cruise ship that’s been dressed up as a dragon. It’s off down the Yangtze at nine miles an hour, through steep-sided maple forests, visiting bleak resort towns before entering the eerie, post-apocalyptic world around the Three Gorges dam. The villages here have all been left in ruins, abandoned save for one lone old hermit who harvests cabbages to boil each evening over an open fire. Weicheng’s documentary has no overt political message; even so, the Royal Splendor’s joyless on-board entertainment is thick with propaganda and it sits harshly against the film’s archive footage of tearful 90s villagers being forcibly boated from their homes. This is a gorgeous, slow-burning, quietly damning piece of work; the tale of a ghost ship travelling through a dead land.

IDFA likes its films to be truly independent. That means no pictures from countries with poor human rights records and limited press freedom. Specifically, this year, that means no state-supported films from Russia, China or Israel. Public events in the likes of Toronto tend to be stage-managed. Here they are fiery and political, small staging posts for the revolution to come, with IDFA positioned as a safe haven for dissident voices. “I come from a country that is governed by the far-right,” says Sofia Bordenave, the Argentinian director of Forest Up in the Mountain, an expose of a policy of state violence against the indigenous Mapuche population. “It is a government that despises thought, knowledge and art. Making documentaries, then, can be an act of resistance. But one of the problems in Argentina is censorship and the lack of cinema screens. So the resistance becomes about showing the problems of Argentina to audiences in festivals around the world. We’re talking to the world but we are unable to talk to our own country.”

Can these documentaries really move the needle, or are they just preaching to the converted? “People talk about films changing the world,” says Yuval Abraham, NAZA’s co-director, who beams into IDFA’s panel discussion via videolink. “I don’t think that a film can really do that. But I think films can definitely be part of a network, of a larger kind of energy that exists in the world and that is pushing for humanity and empathy and change.”

Film festivals typically bill themselves as “festivals of discovery”, full of hidden treasures and exciting wanders in the dark. But sometimes the real discovery can be the festival itself. This was my first time at IDFA; what was I thinking all those years? It’s a fabulous event, impassioned and inclusive. The films in the lineup have generally been terrific: a series of candles or flashlights to guide us through the dark places. Unexpectedly – perhaps perversely – it’s been thoroughly enjoyable, too. What IDFA offers, I suppose, is a kind of reverse escapism, a soul-stirring, suspension-free ride along roads less travelled to hear stories seldom told. It’s been good; I’ll miss it and fear most other films won’t measure up. I’m leaving the real world behind and returning to cheap fiction with a bump.

articles.title: Emery insists no change of plan for Aston Villa despite fears over Galatasaray surface
articles.summary: ‘Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible,’ says Villa manager Turkish champions had to move game on Saturday Unai Emery has insisted he will not alter his plans for Aston Villa’s Champions League game at ­Galatasaray on Tuesday night on account of concerns about the state of the pitch. The Turkish champions hastily moved Saturday’s home fixture from Rams Park after starting emergency repairs to the surface this month. The Villa defender Ian Maatsen said he and his teammates were aware the pitch was in a “bad condition”. Villa were informed by Uefa last week that they would be unable to train at the venue the day before the Champions League game in order to give the pitch maximum time to recover after heavy maintenance work. Galatasaray played Saturday’s victory over Samsunspor at Basaksehir Fatih Terim stadium, a significantly smaller ground named after the former Turkey manager, who played for and managed Galatasaray. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Unai Emery has insisted he will not alter his plans for Aston Villa’s Champions League game at ­Galatasaray on Tuesday night on account of concerns about the state of the pitch. The Turkish champions hastily moved Saturday’s home fixture from Rams Park after starting emergency repairs to the surface this month. The Villa defender Ian Maatsen said he and his teammates were aware the pitch was in a “bad condition”.

Villa were informed by Uefa last week that they would be unable to train at the venue the day before the Champions League game in order to give the pitch maximum time to recover after heavy maintenance work. Galatasaray played Saturday’s victory over Samsunspor at Basaksehir Fatih Terim stadium, a significantly smaller ground named after the former Turkey manager, who played for and managed Galatasaray.

Galatasaray’s manager, Okan Buruk, acknowledged the pitch would pose problems despite round-the-clock efforts to improve the hybrid surface, where sand remains present. “We are not expecting a perfect pitch, but we are at least expecting a pitch that will be playable and will not get any worse or deteriorate during the game,” he said.

Villa instead trained at Bodymoor Heath, their Warwickshire base, on Monday before flying to Istanbul. Villa typically choose to train there before flying to games overseas, though they trained at Fenerbahce on the eve of their Europa League visit in January, and at Besiktas Park 24 hours before their Europa League triumph here in May.

“If we could have trained in the stadium of Galatasaray, maybe we would have decided for the same situation, but it’s not changing our routine,” Emery said. “How the pitch is going to be tomorrow is important, but it’s not an excuse because it’s [the same] for both teams. Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible.”

The Villa manager added: “If the pitch was not available or a risk for the players, for some injuries, we are not playing there. I think it’s going to be [good] enough, well enough to play the match. We are thinking only to face them [Galatasaray] and thinking only to play how we are, not ­changing our idea or our plan for the pitch.”

Victor Osimhen is sidelined for Galatasaray with a knee injury, but the record 26-time Turkish champions expect to welcome back the former Tottenham defender Davinson Sánchez. The former Arsenal midfielder Lucas Torreira and Yunus Akgun, who spent 2023-24 on loan at Leicester, scored in the 2-1 win over Samsunspor, which maintained their three-point lead in the Super Lig.

Buruk was sent off after full-time, after receiving a second yellow card for failing to shake hands with the referee, Ali Sansalan, but his touchline ban does not apply to the Champions League. Galatasaray have appealed to the Turkish Football Federation against the dismissal.

“You can shake hands if you want, or not,” Buruk said. “As long as you don’t show disrespect or use abusive language, no one can punish anyone. The referee made a mistake. I expect that mistake to be reversed.”

articles.content:
Désiré Doué sustained an ACL injury in PSG’s 3-2 win at Nice and joins Khvicha Kvaratskhelia on the treatment table

L uis Enrique is in uncharted territory, even if he insists that “it isn’t a first”. Since arriving at Paris Saint-Germain in 2023, only three players have spent more than 100 days on the sideline – Nuno Mendes, Lucas Hernandez and Presnel Kimpembe – and only Mendes is an important first-team player. But for the remainder of the season, or at least the vast majority of it, Luis Enrique must do without two of his stars: Désiré Doué and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

Doué arrived in Nice on Saturday evening already bearing scars. The PSG forward wore a mouth guard after Davide Frattesi had dislodged one of his front teeth with a stray arm during France’s defeat by Italy during the international break.

He showed it off to the crowd when he tapped home an Achraf Hakimi cross to give PSG a 2-1 lead a mere 24 seconds after Senny Mayulu had levelled the score from the spot for PSG. Just six minutes later, without making any contact with the oncoming Sofiane Diop, Doué was left screaming on the floor, clutching his right knee.

The Nice players Alidu Seidu and Youssouf Ndayishimiye, both of whom have sustained ACL injuries in recent times, quickly grasped the severity of the injury, the nature of which was confirmed on Sunday. Tests revealed an ACL tear that will probably rule Doué out until the end of the season; Kvaratskhelia suffered the same fate last month.

“We have other players in our squad. We will overcome it as a team,” said Luis Enrique , who added that they are “open” to dipping into the market. Eli Junior Kroupi is being linked with a move from Bournemouth to the Parc des Princes, but should the two-time European champions opt against recruiting this winter, it will be a test of the club’s continued assertion that “the star is the collective”. That mantra belies a continued level of spending at PSG that far outstrips their domestic competitors and an accumulation of talent that led Nice’s manager, Olivier Pantaloni, to describe them as a “club apart” in Ligue 1.

Pantaloni noted PSG’s capacity to turn on “at the press of a button”, which left him in no doubt that PSG would “steamroll” the domestic competition once again this year. His side’s 3-2 defeat at their hands, although valiant, reasserts a hierarchy that no one questions, injuries or no injuries.

Ligue 1 may not challenge PSG but, shorn of two of their most technically gifted players, top European sides will. Even in domestic games, wins have oftentimes relied on call-in-the-cavalry hour, with Ousmane Dembélé, Kvaratskhelia, Vitinha and the like unleashed against already exhausted defences to seal the win. Their victories over Le Mans and Strasbourg , notably, were obtained in this manner.

The serious injuries sustained by Doué and Kvaratskhelia mean there is no longer a cavalry to call upon. PSG will also have to change their contentious policy of resting key players in domestic competition. Will Dembélé have to play more, and can his body sustain it? That is one question among many.

Mika Godts has said he has time on his side to establish himself at PSG. Not any more. Will he step up? Will Ferran Torres, who scored PSG’s third in their 3-2 win against Nice, rediscover his early-season form? Is Mayulu, fresh from making his France debut, ready? Is Nuno Mendes a viable option on the left wing? And can Maghnes Akliouche, who has so quickly curried favour with Luis Enrique, add goals and assists to his impressive performances?

The answers to these questions will determine PSG’s ability to challenge for a third consecutive Champions League title. Diminished in quantity and quality, PSG’s forward line no longer looks the best in Europe.

It was the abject failure of the Neymar-Kylian Mbappé-Lionel Messi frontline that forged the concept of the modern-day PSG. Star quality was not a guarantor of success; the system, it was decided, would be king. In the absence of Doué and Kvaratskhelia, the limits of this accepted truth will be tested this season.

Several French clubs used the international break to correct their course. Lens called time on the failed Yannick Cahuzac experiment and brought in Didier Digard, fresh from his sacking at bottom side Le Havre. Strasbourg pulled the plug on Hugo Oliveira after 10 games and hired Vítor Matos from Swansea City to become their fourth manager of 2026. Valérien Ismaël has replaced Digard at Le Havre. And Lyon, whose hand was forced by Paulo Fonseca’s wish to manage boyhood club Sporting, welcomed Carlos Vicens, formerly part of Pep Guardiola’s backroom staff.

Vicens was the only manager to secure all three points on his debut, winning 1-0 at Davide Ancelotti’s Lille. In doing so, the Spaniard became the first manager in Lyon’s history to arrive mid-season and beat a top-flight side in his first away match. Lens showed promise in their 1-1 draw against Toulouse but were denied three points by an inspired performance from goalkeeper Guillaume Restes. There are no signs of revival at Le Havre, who lost 3-1 to promoted side Troyes – or at Strasbourg, who were beaten 1-0 by Brest at the Meinau. Chelsea’s partner club currently occupy the relegation playoff spot.

Five consecutive wins in Ligue 1 had lifted spirits in Marseille , but Bruno Génésio had warned that the revival teetered on a “knife’s edge”. An excellent Le Mans exposed their fragility. Goals from Amine Gouiri and Igor Paixão gave Marseille a 2-0 lead only for Le Mans to run riot in the final quarter of the game and win 3-2.

Patrick Videira’s side secured all three points thanks to Jean Vercruysse’s dramatic 95th-minute winner. “There is a global phenomenon of fragility as soon as we concede a goal,” was Génésio’s explanation for Marseille’s collapse. For Videira, Marseille represent the biggest scalp of his managerial career, although draws against Nice, Lens, and Monaco had already shown the club’s ability to compete at this level.
paragraphs: Désiré Doué sustained an ACL injury in PSG’s 3-2 win at Nice and joins Khvicha Kvaratskhelia on the treatment table

L uis Enrique is in uncharted territory, even if he insists that “it isn’t a first”. Since arriving at Paris Saint-Germain in 2023, only three players have spent more than 100 days on the sideline – Nuno Mendes, Lucas Hernandez and Presnel Kimpembe – and only Mendes is an important first-team player. But for the remainder of the season, or at least the vast majority of it, Luis Enrique must do without two of his stars: Désiré Doué and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

Doué arrived in Nice on Saturday evening already bearing scars. The PSG forward wore a mouth guard after Davide Frattesi had dislodged one of his front teeth with a stray arm during France’s defeat by Italy during the international break.

He showed it off to the crowd when he tapped home an Achraf Hakimi cross to give PSG a 2-1 lead a mere 24 seconds after Senny Mayulu had levelled the score from the spot for PSG. Just six minutes later, without making any contact with the oncoming Sofiane Diop, Doué was left screaming on the floor, clutching his right knee.

The Nice players Alidu Seidu and Youssouf Ndayishimiye, both of whom have sustained ACL injuries in recent times, quickly grasped the severity of the injury, the nature of which was confirmed on Sunday. Tests revealed an ACL tear that will probably rule Doué out until the end of the season; Kvaratskhelia suffered the same fate last month.

“We have other players in our squad. We will overcome it as a team,” said Luis Enrique , who added that they are “open” to dipping into the market. That mantra belies a continued level of spending at PSG that far outstrips their domestic competitors and an accumulation of talent that led Nice’s manager, Olivier Pantaloni, to describe them as a “club apart” in Ligue 1.

Ligue 1 may not challenge PSG but, shorn of two of their most technically gifted players, top European sides will. Even in domestic games, wins have oftentimes relied on call-in-the-cavalry hour, with Ousmane Dembélé, Kvaratskhelia, Vitinha and the like unleashed against already exhausted defences to seal the win. articles.content:
If you’re a cyberpunk who loves ennui and watching actors you can’t see speak words you can’t hear, get stuck in! The rest of us will just be baffled and bored

W hy is James Bond not a TV series by now? Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Alien, Star Wars – all given the TV treatment. Franchise-mining is fantastic business, maximising attention share in order to sell adverts. So why not Bond, which is co-owned by Amazon? Maybe watching a punchy sex addict every week, saying his name with weirdly administrative syntax, might just be … too much?

I entertained these thoughts while struggling to get through another series expansion: Blade Runner 2099 (Prime Video, from Wednesday). I’m a fan of the films. Before the original, cinema had imagined the future as serene and orderly. Blade Runner introduced many of us to novelist Philip K Dick’s vision, in which tech has colonised every aspect of life, but inequality has got worse. Surveillance, artificial beings and unchecked corporate power hollow out whatever remains of society. (The fact the new series is on Amazon is the closest it gets to making a joke.)

As an aside, any title that ends with a “99” risks sounding like a price point, before you factor in the Jeff Bezos of it all. It’s easy to imagine this show interrupted by a jarring, algorithmic voiceover: “The Blade Runner, £20.99, cuts linoleum and vinyl flooring to size, and even cork panels!” Prime Video already offer clickable adverts during streaming, so such cross-promotional revenue streams must be something they’ve considered.

Anyway, the premise is solid. Set 50 years after Denis Villeneuve’s Blade Runner sequel, the series imagines a flipped social order. After ecological catastrophe on Earth, artificial humans have risen up and taken over. Blade runners are now a task force of replicants who hunt rebellious humans. One such human, Cora, infiltrates the LAPD to track down a mysterious item that will expose a huge secret. She’s partnered with a dying blade runner, who’s tracking down a missing officer, who is also looking for … something. The fact is, halfway through the series, I don’t know what’s going on.

To give the creators their due, they haven’t made concessions for TV. I was worried they might stray too far from the tone of the films but they haven’t. If filming science fiction is like arranging an orgy, in that it all depends on establishing an atmosphere, then they have succeeded wildly. There is atmosphere to burn.

The signature 80s, eerie synthscape of the original remains. In fact, it runs through every scene. When planes of alienated noise aren’t slicing across dialogue, there’s a bowel-quivering bass rumble that may well have hindered my houseplants’ growth cycle. When that drops out, it’s replaced by religious-inflected vocalisations or random mechanical clanking. The sound of this show alone could nullify your SSRIs, before you grapple with its themes of grief, isolation and robot apocalypse.

The visuals are starkly industrial, amber-saturated or filled with plumes of smoke. It’s impressive but oppressive, too. Starting each new episode feels like clocking on to a shift at an underground sulphur mine. Time moves slowly. The camera isn’t in a hurry, and neither are the actors. Their spare dialogue is delivered with portentous pauses between lines, as if the existential weight of dystopia has given everyone chronic fatigue. Or they know they have a lot of time to fill. They’re also standing in the dark, a lot. Grimness: too much. Comprehension: too little. Laptop speakers: stuffed.

For me, intensely atmospheric pieces like this work better in a cinema set-up and at film length. For example, I loved Blade Runner 2049’s sweeping canvas, which it owed to Roger Deakins. It ended in snow-blank, abstracted shots that paralleled its themes of birth and moral choice. It stuck the landing. Blade Runner 2099 plunges us into a far darker world, and after four hours I still don’t know why.

Perhaps odd for a TV critic to say, but not everything should be TV. Hunter Schafer, who plays Cora, and Michelle Yeoh, who plays the dying blade runner, are possibly doing great work. I don’t know. If you’re a cyberpunk who mainlines ennui and likes watching actors you can’t see, speaking words you can’t hear, this show may well knock your fishnet socks off. But why spend this much time immersed in a doomed world, when you could open up a window and watch the real one? It’s live!
