articles.title: GTA 6 hacker released on licence with warning 'don't let this happen again'
articles.summary: 21-year-old Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty to the Rockstar Games hack and others he carried out when he was a teenager.
articles.content:
During the trial, the prosecution described Kurtaj as a "leading light" in the teen gang Lapsus$

A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence on the same day as being sentenced to 7 years in prison.

Multiple offender Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, was released from custody with the judge warning him: "Don't let this happen again."

The now 21-year-old hacked several companies and individuals, including GTA 6-maker Rockstar Games, whom he tried to extort after stealing clips of the unfinished game in 2022.

Kurtaj had pleaded guilty last Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

Kurtaj was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

Now, he has been sentenced and released on the same day as the judge considered his hospital stay and remand in prison long enough.

He has been given a Serious Crime Prevention Order which will last five years. It restricts his activity online including barring him from using Telegram and Discord.

City of London Police said the case "highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online".

He hacked Rockstar games, Revolut and Uber while on bail and under police protection in a Travelodge in Bicester.

He was there for protection from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.

With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week.

He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."

The company refused to co-operate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.

Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.8m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.

The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.

He had short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt without a tie.

The Judge Mr Justice Turner told him "you are a very talented young man," and warned him: "Don't let this happen again."

Kurtaj's defence team said he found the online world a more comfortable way of interacting with other people.

"The restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests that are a core feature of ASD [autism spectrum disorder] led him to become preoccupied with the online world where he felt better able to function and exist," they said.

They said he was exposed to people who showed him how to cheat at games and then to "people who were involved in hacking".

During the pandemic, he was "very isolated" and his "connection to Lapsus$ provided him with a sense of community and self-worth that had been absent in his life previously," they added.

Kurtaj's Snapchat posts were the first sign for reporters that he had been released from a secure hospital

Kurtaj and the gang's other hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber used social engineering techniques - tricking people into clicking malicious links or giving up sensitive information - to gain access to internal systems.

Previously, the court heard that during his hack on Uber he posted a picture of a penis as part of his attempts to force the company to pay a ransom.

His hacks on the companies are estimated to have caused around £10m of damage.

Using the data stolen from the firms, he and other members of the gang targeted cryptocurrency investors.

The prosecution argued that the gang stole at least $300,000 (£230,000) from individual victims.

Kurtaj also pleaded guilty to physical assaults on workers while in custody, including multiple biting incidents.

In prison, he was caught with a mobile phone after sending a taunting text message to police and posting updates on Snapchat.

GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history

articles.title: A job that changed me: My last shift as a truck driver was nearly done. Then a man shouted ‘You’re on fire!’
articles.summary: I was 22 and didn’t have a heavy vehicle licence. But I was game, in that ‘I’ll-do-anything-once’ kind of way I only got the job because my boss was desperate. It was peak sales season, November 1978. Our factory in bayside Melbourne had run radio ads featuring an actor pretending to be a burglar boasting how easy it was to rob places that didn’t have our security doors. People wanted their houses fortified for the holidays. Stock requests were flooding in from stores around the city. Our truckie – let’s call him Kelvin – a corpulent alcoholic with a Chopper moustache, had just been jailed for evading road tax. The firm’s accountant, who’d agreed to fill in, wasn’t fit to drive. He coached the local men’s football team and his wife had just run off with its champion goal-kicker. Continue reading...

I was 22 and didn’t have a heavy vehicle licence. But I was game, in that ‘I’ll-do-anything-once’ kind of way

I only got the job because my boss was desperate. It was peak sales season, November 1978. Our factory in bayside Melbourne had run radio ads featuring an actor pretending to be a burglar boasting how easy it was to rob places that didn’t have our security doors. He coached the local men’s football team and his wife had just run off with its champion goal-kicker.

The boss paired me with the work-experience kid, who we called Slim. Picture a 15-year-old with a mousy bob-cut and pimples. He wasn’t exactly sharp but he could lift and carry.

There were two trucks: an old wooden-tray Bedford and a four-ton van. Kelvin hated the Bedford and removed the engine governor to try to blow it up. Somehow it just kept going.

I looked out and saw a man’s hat in the gutter and a guide dog standing on the footpath. The hat’s owner was lying on his back, holding his nose, yelling abuse at the dog. Passersby were abusing us.

We got down, apologising, and helped the man up. The dog looked on insouciantly.

Groaning, Slim handed me the man’s dented hat. I put it awkwardly on the man’s head and apologised again. He thanked me. We put the dog’s harness in his hand and he hobbled off, swearing at the dog.

After that, I avoided the van. The Bedford was bigger and cruder but made you feel like the king of the road. We drove around that month waiting for it to blow, its engine screaming in mechanical agony. There was no power steering and I felt my truckie shoulders developing. The clutch was so heavy I began walking like a pirate with a wooden leg.

I was happy out on the road. Slim would hang his arm out the window and eagerly slap the door while directing me to some grease-pit for lunch. I felt tough. I had a job with importance and responsibility. Operating a big machine made me feel bigger.

Just before Christmas we heard that Kelvin was getting out on a garnishee arrangement with the government. So my days as a truckie were numbered.

My last shift, Christmas Eve, went smoothly until we were almost home. I’d noticed blue smoke trailing behind and thought the truck was just burning oil. But the smoke was thicker now, and blacker.

We’d stopped at the lights on a highway when a window went down in a car and a man’s finger pointed under the truck. He yelled: “You’re on fire!”

I made it in a minute, parked with a screech, jumped down and grabbed the hose while Slim ran around yelling: “The truck’s on fire!” The whole factory downed tools and came out to watch.

It turned out a tarp stuffed behind the cab had wrapped around the rear wheels until friction ignited the tyres and tray.

The fire brigade was spraying foam on the gutted, smouldering truck when the boss approached me. I expected the worst but he was smiling. He’d ordered a new truck, and now insurance would pay for it.

Kelvin was happy too, when the new chrome-heavy Ford automatic arrived in the new year. “You’re not driving it,” he told me pointedly.

After that, when it came to employment opportunities, I was more discriminating. Saying no isn’t always easy. Learning how takes time.

articles.title: Manchester United to appeal against Leny Yoro red card in defeat by Liverpool
articles.summary: Mauricio Pochettino said after game it was ‘never a foul’ ‘No one’s coming to save us,’ admits Kobbie Mainoo Manchester United intend to appeal against the red card Leny Yoro received in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday. The defender was dismissed after fouling Alexander Isak outside the penalty area but Mauricio Pochettino believes the striker would not have reached the ball to take him through on goal against Senne Lammens and therefore it was not worthy of a sending-off . United’s head coach said: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control. Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
Manchester United intend to appeal against the red card Leny Yoro received in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday. The defender was dismissed after fouling Alexander Isak outside the penalty area but Mauricio Pochettino believes the striker would not have reached the ball to take him through on goal against Senne Lammens and therefore it was not worthy of a sending-off .

United’s head coach said: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control. Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul.”

Dominik Szoboszlai scored from the resulting free-kick to give Liverpool the lead and Florian Wirtz doubled the lead three minutes later. Rio Ngumoha and Victor Muñoz completed the scoring as Pochettino lost his first game in charge of United, leaving them 19th in the Premier League.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

“We’re at the lowest we’ve ever been and no one’s coming to save us,” the midfielder Kobbie Mainoo told MUTV. “There’s no helping hands coming so we’ve got to work together and lean on each other and keep working and hopefully it’ll come good.”

Yoro is due to serve a one-match ban at home to Brentford in the Premier League on Saturday. He is available for United’s Champions League match at Sporting on Wednesday.

articles.content:
Italy’s new cover star enjoyed a ‘beautiful’ treble but could not celebrate it after his side threw away two-goal leads three times to draw 4-4 with Atalanta

T his ought to have been a magic moment for Pio Esposito. He had just scored his first Serie A hat-trick, becoming only the third Italian to get one for Inter in the era of three points for a win. The last to do it was Christian Vieri, back in 2003. Two years before Esposito was born.

We will come back to that. Esposito has been drawing premature comparisons to Vieri for some time and especially now after a barnstorming November in which he has scored eight times in five games, including three in two for his country, and two of those as part of a man-of-the-match performance during an upset win against France .

He was the nation’s cover star after that win, variously punching the air, roaring or spreading arms open wide across the front pages of Italy’s sports newspapers. His body language on Sunday night was different. By the end of Inter’s 4-4 draw with Atalanta , Esposito carried the haunted look of a Dickensian protagonist who had just been visited by the ghost of Belgium past.

“I’m really struggling to give an explanation right now,” Esposito told the TV cameras when asked how his team had failed to win a game that they led 2-0, 3-1 and finally 4-2 as late as the 76th minute. “It’s a beautiful thing [to score the hat-trick] but I’m having a hard time enjoying it because we threw two points away.”

A sentiment that can only have been heightened by a sense of history repeating. Esposito’s goals against France had put Italy on course for the quarter-finals of the Nations League. All they needed to do was draw their final group game away to Belgium. Esposito struck again to give them an early lead at the King Baudouin Stadium. And then they collapsed to a 4-1 defeat.

These stories share another recurring character: Charles De Ketelaere. He provided the assists on Belgium’s first and third goals, turning that game on its head in the space of 10 minutes. On Sunday, he was at it again, scoring Atalanta’s second and third goals then winning the penalty from which his teammate Franck Kessié finally equalised in second-half stoppage time.

Even by the standards of this barmy Serie A season, on a weekend that gave us two 5-1 scorelines and a 4-0, this was a preposterous game of football. Inter looked completely in control heading into the final 20 minutes, leading 3-1 thanks to Esposito’s hat-trick.

He might have made it to three before half-time if Marco Sportiello had not denied him from point-blank range when the score was still 1-0. Instead, Esposito had to wait until just after the interval to bag his third, running on to a Marcus Thuram through ball and lifting it over the Atalanta keeper.

None of the three goals were spectacular, but together they illustrated what a menace Esposito has become. For the first, he simply held his spot in the middle of the penalty area after an initial cross was half-cleared, punishing Atalanta’s defence for losing its shape on the second ball. His second was a glancing header at a corner.

In moments like this, it is easy to see why people want to make that link to Vieri, another powerful Inter No 9 who could dominate in the air. But, leaving aside the obvious point that we are comparing a 21-year-old with 13 top-flight goals to a player who won both Serie A’s capocannoniere award and the Pichichi trophy for top scorer in La Liga, is that even the most apt former star to draw parallels with?

Vieri has said that anyone who thinks they are similar “doesn’t understand much about football”, noting that Esposito’s 6ft 3in height and broad-shouldered physique remind him more of Luca Toni.

Esposito’s brothers Salvatore and Sebastiano – both also professional footballers – have compared him to another former Inter player, Edin Dzeko, whom he looked up to while working his way through the club’s academy. There are certainly echoes of the Bosnian in the work he does as an attacking pivot, holding off defenders to make space for runners from midfield.

But Esposito will not be a carbon copy of any player who has gone before him. Part of the thrill of seeing him excel for club and country over the last month has been watching him start to define himself as confidence grows. He played 48 times for Inter last season, yet always was the understudy to Thuram and Lautaro Martínez. This campaign already feels different. He is becoming a main character in his own right.

If only his supporting casts could perform to the same level. Eljif Elmas’s first goal back for Atalanta had been fortuitous, the ball coming back to him after a first scuffed shot was blocked by Federico Dimarco. After Esposito’s third goal, there were 20 minutes in which Maurizio Sarri’s team barely fashioned a chance. Inter contrived to give them a way back in.

De Ketelaere’s first goal came out of the blue, a header from a corner. Was Esposito himself at fault for not being closer to the Belgian as he leapt in a failed attempt to intercept the cross? In any case, Inter responded immediately, Petar Sucic scoring from the penalty spot after Davide Zappacosta fell and handled the ball while trying to cut out a cross from Thuram.

That should have been the end of things, but it wasn’t. Atalanta’s English winger Jonathan Rowe was allowed to twinkle-toe along the byline and flick an outside-of-the-boot pass back to an entirely unmarked De Ketelaere, who smashed home from the middle of the box. Then, in the 90th minute, the Belgian headed the ball on to Alessandro Bastoni’s outstretched arm, earning the spot-kick that Kessié converted.

Had De Ketelaere also fouled Bastoni while challenging for the ball? Inter had a stronger claim that Zappacosta ought to have been shown a red card for his handball. It was the Zappacosta’s blocked cross that wound up falling to Rowe before Atalanta’s third goal.

But Inter’s manager, Cristian Chivu, is not one to indulge that sort of self-pity. His focus after the game was all on his own team’s mistakes, noting that none of the goals they conceded had come in transition but always “ a difesa schierata ” – with defenders in position who ought to have known better how to manage the threats they faced.

“We will learn our lesson,” he said, but Inter fans will want to see words matched by deeds. Their team had already shipped four goals this season, in a home Champions League defeat by Club Brugge. They have conceded 17 in 12 Serie A games.

The time had come to move no from a 38-year-old Francesco Acerbi and 34-year-old Stefan de Vrij this summer, but the current defence is performing far below the standards they previously helped to set. The sight of John Stones on the bench was encouraging after his hamstring troubles but Inter did concede three times in the one game he has started this season, against Udinese.

At least it will be a while before they, and Esposito, have to see De Ketelaere again. Sarri has been getting much better performances from the Belgian since adjusting Atalanta’s formation to make room for him as a No 10 but still hedged his praise at full-time, saying De Ketelaere still needs to perform with greater continuity: “Physically and technically, though, he’s one of the best I have ever coached.”

articles.content:
Cabbage is such a versatile vegetable, and this wintry take on a classic makes the most of its virtues

C abbage will always be a top-tier vegetable in my eyes – it’s so versatile, from braising to roasting, from shredding it into a fritter to slowly cooking into a soup. I love it! This salad started life as a barbecue side dish, with the dressing made in advance and the wedges slowly charred over hot coals. If you’re a year-round barbecuer, then absolutely give this a go, but for everyone else, the oven-roasted version is just as excellent.

When making the dressing, you want the oil to blitz slowly into the egg and flavourings, as if making a mayonnaise, so be patient and gently lift up the stick blender. You could also do this in a mini food processor and slowly drizzle in the oil through the funnel.

Prep 10 min Cook 30 min Serves 2 as a main , 4 as part of a larger meal

1 sweetheart cabbage (about 500g) 120ml olive oil , plus extra for drizzling Sea salt and black pepper 1 large egg yolk 1 lemon 4 anchovies 1 garlic clove , peeled and finely chopped 1 tsp dijon mustard 50g parmesan , finely grated ½ bunch chives , finely chopped A few sprigs flat-leaf parsley , finely chopped

Heat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9. Trim the cabbage, cut it into quarters, then cut each quarter in half. Lay out the wedges in a single layer on a medium roasting tray, drizzle with olive oil, season and massage in well. Roast for 15 minutes, then turn the cabbage pieces over and roast for a further 10-15 minutes, until tender and charred. (Alternatively, cook them in a griddle pan.)

While the cabbage is cooking, make the dressing, for which you’ll need a cup or jug that just fits the head of a stick blender. Put the egg yolk in the cup/jug and squeeze in the lemon juice. Add the anchovies, garlic, mustard and 30g parmesan, then pour in the olive oil and put the stick blender into the cup so the head is touching the base. Blitz for 30 seconds without moving the stick, making sure it stays touching the base of the cup, then slowly move the blender upwards, so the oil starts to blitz into the dressing. Keep going until you have a smooth, thick dressing. Stir in an additional 10g grated parmesan, then season to taste.

When the cabbage is ready, transfer it to a platter and drizzle over the dressing. Scatter with the chopped herbs and the remaining grated parmesan, and serve.

articles.content:
From Heated Rivalry to Harry Potter, popular series are inspiring fan fiction read by thousands online. Now the authors of those online works are getting publishing deals of their own

S hortly after this year’s London book fair , rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for the author of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 2017 and 2018 by user MsKingBean89 on the online platform Archive of Our Own, All the Young Dudes is arguably the most-read work of fan fiction of all time. Now its author will write a trilogy under the pen name BN King, with the first novel, Wolfboy, due to be published in autumn 2027.

This is by no means the first example of fan fiction crossing over into mainstream publishing: the bestselling debut of 2025, Alchemised, also started off as fan fiction based on the Harry Potter series, with some inspiration from The Handmaid’s Tale too. And nearly 15 years earlier, EL James published Fifty Shades of Grey, which began life as Twilight fan fiction before proceeding, in its new guise, to sell millions of copies worldwide.

The appeal for publishers seems obvious enough. The best loved works of fan fiction (or “fics”, as they are known), many of which are multi-chapter epics running to hundreds of thousands of words, are published online, chapter by chapter, to a passionate and hyper-connected audience of readers. Not only do these works inevitably retain echoes of the much-loved creations on which they are based, they also bring with them a ready-made audience, bound by their love of the urtext and buoyed up by the pleasures of collective obsession. Some fics become so popular they beget fandoms of their own, generating fan fiction, fan art and even translations into other languages.

If you have never read a word of fan fiction, if you have never stayed up into the early hours searching for Buffy the Vampire Slayer fics (Buffy/Faith for ever and always), you might be wondering: what could possibly possess thousands of people with jobs, friends and families to spend hours of their time writing stories based on other stories, and hundreds of thousands more to read them? What is drawing a whole new generation of fans to fan fiction through the gateway drug of gay ice-hockey romance Heated Rivalry , with tens of thousands of fics published on Archive of Our Own, and thousands more for the Game Changers book series on which the TV show is based? The answer is simple enough: fan fiction is the cheapest and most easily customisable medium of cultural wish fulfilment.

As a quick glance at any fan fiction platform will tell you, it seems that when you love a particular cultural product, you tend to wish there was more sex in it. Maybe the product itself is sexy in its own right, the chemistry (on screen or on paper) overt and undeniable. Maybe there’s just a hint of sexual tension, or none at all, but a wealth of deeply drawn characters upon which your fandom can project its own most fervent desires. What do you do when you cannot personally strong-arm the author to write a sequel in which your two favourite characters finally give in to the feelings you have long suspected them of harbouring? What do you do when you have neither the time nor the resources to single-handedly script, cast, shoot, produce and professionally edit another season in which the warrior princess and her plucky sidekick finally get together? You turn to fan fiction.

There are other, more obvious, wishes that fan fiction is uniquely equipped to fulfil. You might love a story so much you wish you could be in it. Well, you can be if you’ve got the time and inclination to write fan fiction; all you have to do is include a “self-insert” (or a “Mary Sue”, as they are sometimes less charitably known). You might love everything about a story but wish it had ended differently. Good news! You can write your preferred ending yourself, unless someone else in your fandom has got there first, in which case, even better news! You can have all the satisfaction with none of the work.

At the most basic level, when you love something as much as fandoms love the things they love, you really just wish there was more of it. But to understand why fan fiction matters so much to so many people, we need to look at how it works. The extreme familiarity of the worlds in which fan fiction is set allows for a kind of emotional shorthand, which in turn lets fans play within the bounds of that familiarity or push well beyond it, reimagining scenes and characters and storylines in ways that can be deeply resonant. Not by accident is so much fan fiction queer, regardless of how queer-coded or not the source material may be. And how else to explain the popularity of some of the more dramatic subcategories that exist within fan fiction? There are hurt/comfort fics, where a character suffers deep emotional or physical trauma and is comforted by another character; or “character death” fics, where a character dies and everyone is really, really sad about it; or that wonderful catch-all “angst”, in its many permutations (“‘light angst”, “heavy angst”, “angst and smut”, “angst with a happy ending”) … When you’re reading fan fiction, you’re invested before you’ve even seen the first word. This makes for a very specific reading experience: it’s reading for emotional gratification. It’s instant, it’s cathartic, and it leaves you wanting more. And all of this material is created and made available for free, with (at least in theory) no motivation other than a shared love of the original work that started it all off.

But as the monetisation of fan fiction continues apace, the inevitable backlash and soul-searching have begun. Specific to the Harry Potter fandom is a discomfort with the possibility that even fan fiction rewritten as original fiction might draw new readers to the books themselves, helping JK Rowling to bankroll what many see as a campaign against transgender rights. More generally, there is a sense that in its desire to make the most of the fan fiction bandwagon, the publishing industry is rerouting opportunities that might otherwise have gone to first-time writers of original fiction. And on a philosophical level, the commercial prospecting of fan fiction feels to some like a betrayal of the very essence of the form. Fan fiction is supposed to be a labour of love – not just for those who write it, but for those who read it, too (for not every fic is a masterpiece, and much clumsy prose must be endured). What will become of fan fiction if people start writing it in the hope they might someday be able to sell their work to a publisher? How will that influence the kinds of things they write, and their relationship with the online communities on whose support they depend?

Already there are signs of some of the difficulties that plague traditional publishing, such as allegations of AI use, and a preoccupation with “reader engagement”. Meanwhile, in a turn of events that may seem – to the more fatalistically inclined – like a harbinger of endtimes, AO3 was recently taken down for more than two weeks as a result of a “security incident”. The website is more or less back up now, but the internet’s reactions during its downtime, ranging from the tongue-in-cheek to the genuinely distressed, demonstrate one thing: people need their fan fiction. Publishing trends come and go, but fan fiction in its many incarnations – from the re-imagined myths of Ovid’s Metamorphoses to 1960s Star Trek fanzines, to the present day – has been around for ever. As long as there are stories, books, movies and TV shows, there will be fandoms. And as long as there are fandoms, there will be fan fiction.

articles.title: You Can See Everything passes $100m at global box office as UK release starts strong
articles.summary: The documentary from Nathan Fielder following fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her imprisonment has broken box office records in the UK Elizabeth Holmes film You Can See Everything has crossed the $100m mark at the global box office as it recorded the highest ever opening weekend figure for a non-music documentary in the UK. Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything earned an estimated $2.5m over the weekend on its sixth week of release in North America, according to Box Office Mojo , bringing its total there to $93.5m. This has been augmented by successful releases in a number of international territories, which has added an estimated $9m for a total of $102.5m. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The documentary from Nathan Fielder following fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her imprisonment has broken box office records in the UK

Elizabeth Holmes film You Can See Everything has crossed the $100m mark at the global box office as it recorded the highest ever opening weekend figure for a non-music documentary in the UK.

Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything earned an estimated $2.5m over the weekend on its sixth week of release in North America, according to Box Office Mojo , bringing its total there to $93.5m. This has been augmented by successful releases in a number of international territories, which has added an estimated $9m for a total of $102.5m.

This means the film is already the seventh highest grossing documentary of all time, in a list currently headed by the 2009 film Michael Jackson’s This Is It on $267.9m. In North America alone, it is now the third highest grossing documentary, behind Fahrenheit 9/11 and Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour.

Despite releasing a month and a half later, the UK has seen stellar figures on the film’s first weekend in cinemas. Variety reports it took an estimated $3.2m (£2.4m) from more than 590 venues, itself a record for a non-music documentary.

You Can See Everything has proved to be a significant commercial success for its backers, which include distribution outfit A24, with the film reportedly costing $7m to make.

articles.content:
Four-year-old me had never worried about fashion fails or making a fool of myself. It was time to ditch this grown-up obsession with getting everything right

I ’ve always been a perfectionist. As a student, I have spent months worrying about assignments long after submitting them, and criticised myself over tiny things such as making spelling mistakes in birthday cards. When I speak to friends or strangers, I’m so focused on not saying the “wrong” thing that I forget to enjoy chatting with them.

As part of gen Z, I know there is a wider culture of fear among my generation: I’m not the only one worried about doing or saying something that is embarrassing or, God forbid, cringe .

In avoiding mistakes, it struck me that I had become afraid of doing anything at all. I’ve abandoned hobbies I used to enjoy, such as writing poetry, because I worried it might be seen as “naff”. I stopped playing the violin because I didn’t want to make a fool of myself when practising in student halls.

As I turned 21, I realised that I didn’t want to carry this mindset with me for the rest of my life. The solution came to me unexpectedly one night over dinner with friends, when we began scrolling through photos and videos of our childhood. After the initial hilarity about our poor fashion choices and bad camera angles, I noticed something I had forgotten: my younger self had a remarkable sense of freedom.

Four-year-old me wore bright green socks with pink sandals without worrying about making a fashion “fail”. When, at the age of seven, I wrote songs with my brother and cousin, we didn’t aspire to write a hit single, but just enjoyed the process of creating something together. I began to wonder whether the best antidote for perfectionism in adulthood was to revisit the time before it existed.

Soon, whenever I caught myself being critical or avoiding things out of fear of making a mistake, I began to think about what my younger self would make of the situation.

When I moved to Copenhagen for a year abroad in 2025 as part of my university degree, cycling everywhere – as Danish people do – felt like a terrifying, insurmountable hurdle. Despite familiarising myself with the rules, I was worried about navigating busy traffic, and almost gave up on it altogether. Then I remembered how I’d learned to ride a bike much later than most of my classmates. When I was 10, cycling didn’t come naturally to me, but I kept trying because making mistakes never felt like a reason to give up.

I realised that if this version of me knew that I was even considering cycling abroad, she would be so excited. I started on quiet streets near my accommodation, before gradually exploring the whole city. Instead of expecting myself to be perfect, I just enjoyed the experience.

A similar shift happened with my friends. Because they are all so smart, I often overthought things I said in conversations with them. But remembering the 10-year-old version of me, who always felt slightly out of place but hoped for a group of friends that would feel like my family, suddenly made just being with them feel like enough.

I also began to use music to connect with my childhood self, rediscovering songs that my dad used to play in the car when I was young. The more I let my younger self back into my life, the less power perfectionism seems to have over me. Realising that I am not just achieving but surpassing the small dreams she once had has reminded me to stop measuring every moment against my impossible standards. As a teenager, I thought that becoming an adult meant leaving my childhood self behind – but now I can’t wait to bring her along for the ride.

I ’ve always been a perfectionist. As a student, I have spent months worrying about assignments long after submitting them, and criticised myself over tiny things such as making spelling mistakes in birthday cards. When I speak to friends or strangers, I’m so focused on not saying the “wrong” thing that I forget to enjoy chatting with them.
As part of gen Z, I know there is a wider culture of fear among my generation: I’m not the only one worried about doing or saying something that is embarrassing or, God forbid, cringe .

In avoiding mistakes, it struck me that I had become afraid of doing anything at all. I’ve abandoned hobbies I used to enjoy, such as writing poetry, because I worried it might be seen as “naff”. I stopped playing the violin because I didn’t want to make a fool of myself when practising in student halls.

Soon, whenever I caught myself being critical or avoiding things out of fear of making a mistake, I began to think about what my younger self would make of the situation.

articles.title: Sounds may seem louder or even painful as you age. Here’s why
articles.summary: For some, everyday loud noise becomes bothersome. Researchers call this sound hypersensitivity and it’s worth knowing whether it’s due to ageing or not Loud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t. Continue reading...
articles.content:
For some, everyday loud noise becomes bothersome. Researchers call this sound hypersensitivity and it’s worth knowing whether it’s due to ageing or not

L oud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t.

For some people, everyday sounds become hard to bear. Some researchers call this sound hypersensitivity , an umbrella term for several conditions.

There’s some disagreement about the names and definitions of these conditions, which makes it hard to determine how common they are. One of them is noise sensitivity, a tendency to feel annoyed or overwhelmed by ongoing background noise. Others include hyperacusis, in which ordinary sounds feel uncomfortably loud or even painful; misophonia, or intense anger, disgust or anxiety in response to specific sounds (For example: another person’s breathing); and phonophobia, the fear that a sound will cause discomfort.

Scientists don’t fully understand why everyday sounds become hard to tolerate for certain people. Daniel Polley, a neuroscientist who directs the Lauer Tinnitus Research Center at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, suspects some of the discomfort is a natural response to an increasingly industrialized and noisy world full of sounds we can’t control.

“As we age, we get a bit more rigid about what it is that we want going into our bodies,” he says, “including sound waves”.

That said, researchers are investigating a range of possible explanations. They haven’t pinned down a brain change that explains any one type of sound hypersensitivity, but people at higher risk for certain types include those with hearing loss, tinnitus (chronic ringing or buzzing in the ears), and neuropsychiatric conditions like autism. Much of what’s known about possible mechanisms of sound hypersensitivity comes from rodent studies, so there are still big questions about what’s happening in people.

A leading theory is called central gain , which relates to hearing loss. According to this theory, when damage to the inner ear weakens the signal it sends to the brain, the brain turns up its own amplification to compensate. As a result, it perceives a small increase in volume as much larger, which makes sounds seem louder than they really are. “The perception of sound isn’t generated in the ear; it’s generated in the brain,” says Polley.

Possible triggers are changes to the inner ear caused by age, noise exposure, or both. These can result in the loss of cells that amplify sound, and fraying of the auditory nerve that carries those cells’ signals to the brain.

Some people with sound hypersensitivity have hearing loss they don’t know about. Routine testing may not clarify things either, because standard hearing tests don’t pick up auditory nerve damage. As a result, some people with this type of hearing loss may struggle to follow conversations in noisy places but pass a hearing test.

There’s no medication that reliably eliminates sound hypersensitivity or reverses inner ear damage. However, certain strategies can lower your risk and ease symptoms.

The most important preventive step is to protect your ears from loud noise. Long or repeated exposure to sounds at 85 decibels or more , like those from speaker-heavy concerts , lawnmowers and leaf blowers, can damage your hearing. Wearing ear protection can delay that damage, although some wear comes with age no matter what.

If you suspect you already have some sound hypersensitivity, noise-canceling earbuds can quickly cut loud background noise while still letting you hear sounds you choose, says Polley. Earplugs also work, but they block everything, including sounds you may need or want to hear.

Just be aware that overprotecting your hearing can backfire. Shutting out too much sound may prompt the brain to turn up its amplification even further, which can worsen sound hypersensitivity. In one small study, people with normal hearing who wore earplugs for two weeks became less tolerant of loud sounds . “Isolating yourself, like going monastic, is not necessarily the right approach,” says Polley.

In one trial, people who did cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) tolerated louder sounds . This type of talk therapy can help sufferers avoid sounds less, face uncomfortable sounds gradually and feel less threatened by them. Some kinds of sound hypersensitivity are closely tied to anxiety and depression , and it’s possible treating those conditions can reduce symptoms.

Get help if sound hypersensitivity is causing you a lot of anxiety, disrupting your sleep or getting in the way of daily life, says Polley. Audiologists are usually the first point of contact. They can test your hearing and refer you to other specialists if needed.

If sounds hurt your ears, you may require a more cautious treatment approach . See a clinician, who may order brain imaging to rule out a growth on the auditory nerve.

If you have tinnitus, mention it to your clinician, as it often comes with sound hypersensitivity. Also take note if only one ear is affected; this may point to a specific cause that needs attention.

articles.title: How to make nasi goreng – recipe | Felicity Cloake's Masterclass
articles.summary: The richly flavoured Indonesian and Malaysian fried-rice dish is quick to cook, but calls for a little groundwork. Here’s how to make it Unless you’ve had the admirable foresight to prepare the spice paste in advance, thus turning this into just a quick assembly job, nasi goreng is not a fried rice that you whip up in five minutes from last night’s leftovers. Neither, however, is it particularly complex, and the richly savoury, shallot-sweet base gives it a depth of flavour that more than justifies the modest investment of time. Prep 25 min Chill 2 hr+ Cook 5 min Serves 2 Continue reading...
articles.content:
The richly flavoured Indonesian and Malaysian fried-rice dish is quick to cook, but calls for a little groundwork. Here’s how to make it

U nless you’ve had the admirable foresight to prepare the spice paste in advance, thus turning this into just a quick assembly job, nasi goreng is not a fried rice that you whip up in five minutes from last night’s leftovers. Neither, however, is it particularly complex, and the richly savoury, shallot-sweet base gives it a depth of flavour that more than justifies the modest investment of time.

200g jasmine rice , or other long-grain rice, or 525g cooked and cooled rice 2 tbsp neutral oil 1 garlic clove , peeled and finely chopped 2 eggs , beaten (optional) 2 tbsp kecap manis (see step 5) 1 tbsp light soy sauce 4 spring onions , trimmed and chopped on the diagonal 1 bird’s eye chilli , sliced, to serve

For the paste 50g Asian red shallots (about 4) 1 garlic clove 1 red bird’s eye chilli , or similar 1 tbsp neutral oil 2 tsp terasi (Indonesian shrimp paste; see step 4)

Optional toppings Crispy shallots (bought or homemade) Fried eggs Sliced cucumber or tomatoes Lightly blanched vegetables Cooked meat or seafood or cubed tofu or tempeh Salted peanuts , roughly chopped

Should you happen to have cooked and cooled long-grain rice ready to use, start at step 3; the amount suggested above is fairly elastic, and the recipe easily scaled up or divided. If you’re cooking rice (preferably jasmine, but any long-grain variety will do) specially, put it in a pan with 400ml boiling water, then bring to a simmer, stirring once.

Cover the pan tightly and turn the heat right down. Cook for 15 minutes, then take off the heat and place on a damp tea towel or cloth for five minutes. Fluff the rice with a fork, then spread it on a baking tray and put in the fridge to cool and dry out, ideally overnight, or for up to two hours in the freezer.

If you can’t find small, fiery Asian shallots, use 75g of the larger round ones instead, to compensate for their milder flavour. Peel and roughly chop the shallots and garlic. Trim the chilli (remove and discard the pith and seeds if you’re nervous of heat, or use a milder variety instead), then roughly chop and put in a mortar or mini chopper.

Add the oil and terasi (Malaysian belacan , Thai kapi or Vietnamese mắm tôm make good substitutes for this Indonesian fermented shrimp paste); if you can’t find any of them, use a teaspoon and a half of fish sauce and two anchovy fillets (or two teaspoons of red miso mixed with a teaspoon of crumbled dried seaweed ) . Pound or whizz until smooth.

Kecap manis is a thick, sweet soy sauce that’s easily found in specialist Asian food shops and online. To make your own, put four tablespoons of light soy sauce in a small pan with the same amount of soft brown sugar, simmer until reduced to a slightly syrupy consistency, then leave to cool and use in the recipe below (note: this will make more than you need).

Prepare the toppings according to taste; nasi goreng exists in countless permutations across Indonesia and Malaysia, so it’s a great home for leftovers and various odds and ends from the vegetable drawer. Like many fried dishes, this one comes together fast, so have everything ready and within easy reach of the hob before you even think about starting the cooking.

Put the oil in a wok on a high heat, then fry the chopped garlic until just lightly golden. Pour in the eggs, if using, leave to cook until half set, then break up. Carry on scrambling until the eggs are just beginning to brown, then stir in the spice paste and cook for another minute or so.

Once the shallots in the paste have lost their raw smell, sprinkle in the rice by hand, breaking up any clumps as you go, then stir-fry, tossing vigorously, until it’s thoroughly heated through. Stir in the kecap manis, soy sauce and chopped spring onion, ensuring the grains are brown and evenly coated with sauce.

Fry, stirring, for another minute or so, until the rice is just beginning to caramelise and crisp, then taste and season as necessary with more kecap manis and chilli. Divide between plates and top with the sliced chilli and crispy shallots, if using, plus your chosen accompaniments. Serve immediately.

articles.title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
articles.summary: After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11 . She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California. Continue reading...
articles.content:
After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack

Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11 .

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage . She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California.

“I presumed there had been a hack of the aviation system and that it would be down for days,” she said.

Instead, flights resumed later that day and Reindorf was able to make the wedding even if she missed that night’s rehearsal dinner. But passengers appeared to be convinced of two things, she said: “That it was a cyber-attack and that we were not going to be told the truth about it.”

This was not an isolated view. What happened in the days after the incident, which began on Thursday 12 November, left many wondering if the US, and the western world, was under a coordinated assault. By Tuesday big US banks , Apple , and the National Security Agency had also been affected by technical glitches. Researchers also flagged a cyber-attack that targeted 178 organisations worldwide , although the financial losses appeared to be small.

The truth is more prosaic. The chaos of the previous weeks – grounded planes, frozen email servers, iPhone outages – appears, on closer examination, to be more a string of coincidences than anything else, in part driven by fears over advancing artificial intelligence.

But the narratives that have sprung up around it are a measure of an unstable and frenetic global mood, which is dealing with two powerful trends: the rot of decades-old infrastructure from chronic underinvestment and the genesis of some of the most powerful technology humanity has made – AI.

The failure that delayed Reindorf’s takeoff originated with a faulty router in the city of El Dorado, Arkansas, population 16,609.

That router was installed in the midst of a maintenance procedure that has been under way for more than two decades. In 2002, the US government contracted a small company, now known as L3Harris, to modernise the communications system of the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA), in charge of America’s airports. As a part of it, L3Harris has been tearing up communication lines made of copper wire across the country, and replacing them with fibre optic cables.

This glacial undertaking sparked a sudden and unprecedented catastrophe – the router, newly replaced, misfired and caused air traffic communications across the US to crash, bringing all departing flights nationwide to a grinding halt. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled.

L3Harris’s contracts, which have now run into the billions of dollars, are one emblem of where the world is today: mired in ageing infrastructure that is slowly failing, yet immensely costly to replace.

There is a broad sense that governments everywhere are not equipped to deal with this. In the US, oversight reports have been urgently calling for upgrades to the FAA for years. The FAA only announced that it would phase out the use of decades-old floppy discs containing vital weather and other critical information just last year.

Meanwhile, there are more subtle issues around other incidents, such as the Microsoft outage. An upgrade in July left in place a software bug that lurked quietly for months before a string of coincidences triggered it – overwhelming the company’s servers and halting the use of most of Microsoft’s systems worldwide. The outage halted everyday procedures such as the release of detainees in American jails and access to some patients records at UK hospitals .

It was accompanied by more chaos. A software bug at JP Morgan Chase, the largest bank in the US, delayed transactions, a disruption that rippled throughout the country’s banks and their customers. An internal update at Apple caused outages of some of its iPhone apps. Routine maintenance went awry at the US Department of Defense’s National Security Agency (NSA), temporarily disrupting the internal network the agency uses to send and receive classified information.

Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and Apple might have moved far beyond copper wire and floppy discs, mostly, but they – and software companies everywhere – have been forced to run at double the pace in recent months, because of a deluge of bugs being discovered by AI. This might not be the specific reason for those upgrades; some maintenance is routine.

But AI-driven hacking has ushered in a new reality for IT professionals. The NSA told Congress that its communication outage was a result of quick fixes to systems identified as vulnerable by AI.

To recap: this spring, Anthropic and OpenAI both released powerful AI models capable of finding bugs in lines of code. One senior cybersecurity professional told the Guardian the relentless exposure of IT flaws had left their team “exhausted”.

AI helped to uncover a bug in the PHP programming language in October. This was followed by the discovery of a vulnerability in the Java programming language on Tuesday, followed by another bug in NGINX, a web server.

“When NGINX happened I thought, ‘Oh come on – another one?’,” said the professional.

Java and PHP are both part of the essential backbone of the internet, vital infrastructure that keeps most of the world online.

“AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery so rapidly that organisations are applying patches at a volume and pace their systems were never built to absorb,” said Jamieson O’Reilly, a cybersecurity specialist.

Tech companies are constantly finding potential bugs and fixing them. Now they have to do it a lot faster, said O’Reilly: “The volume and speed of AI-driven discovery makes their problems far more acute.”

The backdrop to all this was a cybersecurity narrative already running at a fraught pitch due to the hacks of supermarket fridges across Europe, global scares such as the discovery of the flaw in PHP and the multibillion-dollar hack of the Binance cryptocurrency exchange .

Social media filled the gaps where organisations could not immediately supply information. Laura Loomer , a prominent conspiracy peddler, posted on X that “we are clearly being attacked by foreign adversaries via cyber-attacks”, adding “go get cash”. On TikTok, there are posts about a #90daypoweroutage, a conspiracy theory sparked by a nationwide test of the US emergency alert system – and a Simpsons clip .

The consequences of conspiratorial thinking can be seen at Costco, a bulk-buying retailer, where there has been a rise in emergency prep sales including purchases of generators, and general “pantry-loading” in the UK. Analysts at Mizuho Bank said this was a result of “consumer anxiety” following the outages and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media”.

These concerns have not been confined to the fringes. The UK government recently told its citizens to stock up on three days’ worth of cash, among other basic items , as part of a readiness-for-crisis campaign.

Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, whose research centres on the spread of myths and misinformation, said the “clustering” of events such as multiple outages “can be perceived as being indicative of purposeful coordination rather than chance”.

Feeding into the anxiety, there have also been examples of state and criminal actors causing disruption, from Russia targeting undersea internet cables to last year’s crippling of Britain’s biggest carmaker, Jaguar Land Rover , which give credence to public concerns. A solution, said Lewandowsky, was “for responsible governments to be transparent and accurate in their communications” in order to suppress wilder explanations.

Taken together, experts say that the string of outages highlights the stunning fragility of US and global infrastructure, where a single mistake or malfunction can bring entire transportation, communication, and security systems to a standstill.

“We’ve built a world in which essential systems are so interconnected that a failure in one can just cascade through those systems really quickly,” said Aarathi Krishnan, the founder of Raksha Intelligence Futures, a global intelligence firm. “All of our systems, whether it’s comms, finance, capital, all of it, are so interconnected and concentrated, it creates a dependence. And that dependence creates fragility.”

What can be done? It is unclear. AI-driven bug discovery is not going to slow down and the legacy systems the world is grappling with are what they are. Infrastructure is the often overlooked backbone of society and those who decades ago built networks of road and air traffic systems and electrical grids could not have anticipated these modern threats.

Mike Chapple, the faculty director of Notre Dame University’s business computer science programme, said it was “unfortunate” that one faulty router could have such an effect on a nation’s aviation communication system.

“That just points to a design that isn’t resilient – it shouldn’t be designed in a way that one failure at one location can cause the whole nationwide system to come tumbling down.”

“For myself and many others, we struggled to access life-saving medication,” she said. “It is alarming there was no contingency plan.”

articles.title: How to start volunteering: ‘There are roles to fit all interests and skill sets’
articles.summary: Common misconceptions are that you don’t have the right skills, or you need to make a huge time commitment Many people want to do good in the world. They want to connect and give back to their communities. But volunteering, much like Sunday meal prep or morning meditations , often ends up at the bottom of the to-do list – a nice idea we’ll get to when we have more time. “For many people, volunteering is something they feel positively about, but don’t always prioritize or think they have time for,” says Matt Bertram, vice-president of volunteer services for the American Red Cross. How to start meditating How to start weightlifting How to start budgeting How to start running Continue reading...
articles.content:
Common misconceptions are that you don’t have the right skills, or you need to make a huge time commitment

M any people want to do good in the world. They want to connect and give back to their communities. But volunteering, much like Sunday meal prep or morning meditations , often ends up at the bottom of the to-do list – a nice idea we’ll get to when we have more time.

“For many people, volunteering is something they feel positively about, but don’t always prioritize or think they have time for,” says Matt Bertram, vice-president of volunteer services for the American Red Cross.

Common misconceptions about volunteering, he says, are that you don’t have the right skills to contribute, or that you have to make a huge time commitment.

“In reality, there are many flexible volunteer roles to fit all interests and skill sets,” he says.

There are mental and physical benefits to volunteering. According to a 2023 paper , these include reduced mortality and increased functioning, as well as less tangible benefits like increased quality of life, pride, empowerment, motivation, social support and sense of community.

First, think about the causes or issues you care about. And think broadly.

“The sense of what counts as volunteering has shifted,” says Boram Kim, vice-president for volunteer and institutional engagement at Habitat for Humanity International. Volunteering is no longer limited to traditional, formal roles through large, international organizations. “Increasingly, people mobilize around smaller, immediate issues close to home and within their own communities,” she explains.

After Covid arrived, the number of mutual aid organizations in the US ballooned from 50 to 800, according to the National Education Association . These groups are diverse: some run food pantries, while others help with disaster relief or exchange services and resources. Find a group in your area through directories like Mutual Aid Hub in the US, or Mutual Aid in the UK.

Whether you’re interested in volunteering with a large organization or a small local group, consider your motivation and what you hope to gain from the experience.

“For some, it’s a chance to build skills or strengthen their community, while for others it’s about social connection,” says Kim. “The most essential thing to consider is [the organization’s] alignment with the issues that matter more to [the volunteer].”

As you look at groups and organizations that appeal to you, be realistic about how much time and energy you can offer.

“Keep in mind that every organization has unique needs,” says Julie Sonenberg, senior manager of volunteer engagement at the ASPCA Adoption Center. “Try to find alignment with what you’re able to contribute and what the organization’s needs are.”

When you find a group or organization you like, check their website for volunteer signup information or, if this doesn’t exist, send them an email expressing your interest and availability.

“Once people have a good idea of where and how they want to volunteer, they shouldn’t be afraid to reach out to organizations they are passionate about,” says Kyle Gardner, senior vice-president of development at Charity Navigator.

If you ultimately don’t have the time to volunteer, Gardner suggests contributing in other ways, like setting up recurring donations to a charity, or donating items like food, clothes or furniture.

“One mistake people make when it comes to volunteering is underestimating their skills,” says Kim. People often assume they need specific expertise or skills to contribute, when in fact, “compassion and reliability are the most valuable assets”, he says.

Volunteering can involve hands-on work, but some roles focus on advocacy, fundraising, digital support or storytelling.

At the ASPCA, for example, people often assume “opportunities to volunteer are only available inside a shelter”, Sonenberg says. Such opportunities may entail walking dogs, folding laundry, greeting visitors or cleaning. But the organization also needs advocacy volunteers to help mobilize people and improve laws for animals, and first responders to help animals in crisis.

Many non-profit organizations – including some large, well-known organizations, like the American Red Cross – depend on volunteers to operate. “About 90% of our workforce are volunteers,” Bertram says.

Contributing to a blood drive, supporting community-preparedness events or serving in a virtual or on-call role all make a difference. “Some volunteers contribute just a few hours a month, and that support still makes a real difference,” he says.

Volunteering is also a good reminder that, as helpless as we may feel, our actions can make a difference.

“In my work, I see volunteers transform just as much as the communities they serve,” he says. “Volunteering is a pathway to connection, to each other, to our communities, and to the belief that we can shape a better world.”

articles.title: World Cup 2026: England frustrated; Scotland face Brazil; Infantino defends hydration breaks – live
articles.summary: ⚽ All the latest news on a day packed with six matches ⚽ Player guide | Bracketology | Golden Boot | Mail Daniel How do we feel about the penalty that wasn’t? I don’t really see how you can’t give it. Fatawu was in and Konsa launches into him, getting nowhere near the ball with no chance of getting at the ball – which makes it a red card too. Continue reading...
articles.content:
At the start of the competition, it didn’t look like a 1-0 win and two one-goal defeats would be enough for Scotland, but now, that seems likely to qualify them. However, Brazil looked much better in their second game than their first – admittedly against far worse opposition, but it did also look like Carlo Ancelotti is clover to finding his best team. Against Morocco, I was shocked to see Igor Thiago selected ahead of Matheus Cunha; I think we can safely say that will not happen again.

Which I guess brings us to our next round of action. Before we properly dig in, let’s acquaint ourselves with the panoply of permutations.

Colombia played pretty well, I thought, and would’ve won by more were it not for Lionel Mpasi in the DRC net. I was disappointed by the winner because on first look, I thought Daniel Muñoz had done him with the eyes, but it turned out to be a deflection.

Panama have come on loads since England clattered them in 2018 – Ghana also got away with it against them. Luka Modric, though, what a player.

Qatar’s manager, Julen Lopetegui, has revealed Assim Madibo spent the eve of their final Group A match visiting Ismael Kone after the Canada midfielder underwent successful surgery for a broken leg.

Madibo was sent off after inadvertently injuring Kone in last week’s 6-0 defeat to Canada. At the time Madibo was visibly distraught and he has since visited Kone in Vancouver, Canada’s base for the tournament. Kone, who plays in Serie A for Sassuolo, is expected to miss at least five months of action. “It has been very tough for him,” Lopetegui said of Madibo on Tuesday afternoon. “We wish him [Kone] all the best to recover as soon as possible. “Now in the current moment Madibo is in Vancouver visiting Kone because he was very, very affected by this injury – it was never his intention. It was a very clear accident. We wish him all the best.” Madibo is suspended for Qatar’s match against Bosnia and Herzegovina in Seattle on Wednesday. Homam Ahmed is also suspended after being sent off in the same game last Thursday.

Iran prepared for their final Group G match by highlighting the US’s deadly attack on a school that killed at least 168 people, predominantly schoolchildren. Iran’s players trained at their base in Tijuana, Mexico, on Tuesday evening with black corner flags adorned with the message: “#168” . The number refers to the victims who were killed in a strike on an elementary school in Minab, southern Iran, on 28 February, the first day of the US-Israel war on Iran. The attack was attributed to the US military, with Donald Trump last week saying: “Nobody did that on purpose. Mistakes are made. The war is nasty.” When Iran first landed at their base in Mexico earlier this month, after a training camp in Turkey, they arrived wearing pin badges on their lapels that read: “#168”. Iran will arrive in Seattle from Tijuana at 11.30am local time on Wednesday before facing Egypt on Friday after being granted special permission to arrive in the US two days before the game. The match is the World Cup’s designated Pride Match, despite both teams complaining to Fifa about the celebrations which will coincide with Seattle’s Pride weekend. After Sunday’s draw with Belgium, Iran left a handwritten note in the dressing room at Los Angeles Stadium in which they called for peace. The message, which also featured #168, read: ““From the ancient Persia of thousands of years ago to the civilised Iran of today, the spirit of Iran remains alive and steadfast. We came to Los Angeles with pride, competed with honour, and leave with dignity “Thank you Los Angeles for your hospitality. And thank you to every Iranian who gave their heart, voice and soul for Iran throughout these 180 minutes. May peace, respect and friendship prevail among all nations.”

Fifa’s view of Iran training with #168 flags remains to be seen. Their regulations state that “equipment must not have any political, religious or personal slogans, statements or images” or players and/or the team may be sanctioned by the competition organiser.

Iran were only permitted to arrive in LA before draws against New Zealand and Belgium 24 hours before the games, leading their head coach, Amir Ghalenoei to label Iran the “most oppressed” team at the tournament.

Also at training on Tuesday, the former Brighton winger Alireza Jahanbakshsh was given a commemorative Iran shirt after reaching 100 caps for his country against Belgium. Fifa has been contacted for comment.

I don’t want to get all conspiracist, but you don’t have be John Le Carré to wonder if TV companies benefitting from ad revenue has an upside for Fifa even though they’re not cut in on each specific deal.

This has fuelled debate over their impact on the game, with some viewers complaining about ⁠being exposed to commercials during the three-minute stoppages.

“There is no additional revenue for Fifa, as all ​commercial agreements were signed well in advance. ‌So, this is not ‌a financial issue for us. For us, it is purely a sporting matter,” Infantino said in ‌a statement on Wednesday.

The breaks allow coaching staff to give in-game tactical instructions, a shift critics say disrupts match momentum and fundamentally alters the nature of the game.

England manager Thomas Tuchel said the additional break “interrupts and changes the identity of the football match“, while Uruguay coach Marcelo Bielsa said dividing matches into shorter segments takes away the fundamental characteristic ‌of the game.

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Netherlands captain Virgil van Dijk have supported the intent behind the rule in extreme heat, but questioned ​the need for it in cooler conditions and at covered venues.

“The main reason is the heat, but we also have to understand that in a competition like the (FIFA) World Cup, played over 39 days, with teams potentially playing eight matches in those 39 days, having a moment to rest ⁠is extremely important,” Infantino said.

“What matters even more to us is ensuring ​that all teams, in every ​match, are playing under the ​same conditions.

“It’s very difficult to accept that a coach might have the opportunity ​to influence a ‌match by making adjustments ​simply because it’s ​hotter, while in another match, where the temperature is slightly lower, the same coach doesn’t have the same opportunity.”

Infantino added that the breaks had not reduced the intensity of matches, suggesting players were able to maintain a high level of performance throughout games.

This stodgy draw against Ghana however is exactly how I expect England to play. Remember 0-0 against Algeria? The USA? Remember 2018, when Emmanuel Macron got drenched as Vladimir Putin relaxed under an umbrella held for him? How will Trump assert himself to this level?

Email! “‘I don’t care about Messi’ was such an insulting and insensitive remark from such a talented player,” says Krishnamoorthy V of Ronaldo. “This is what ego does to your personality. Ghana sending CR7 and co home will be so satisfying.”

Jacob makes a fair point here, that Palmer and Foden didn’t do enough to force their way into the squad. But both are special talents who’ve shown quality miles beyond that which we’ve seen from Madueke and Gordon, who are not, and neither of whom were all that good last season either.

Again, though, I come back to the big-space/small-space thing, and the lack of balance in the squad. And, judging by the substitutions, it’s not something management see as an issue – the changes were like for like, rather than seeking to alter or vary the method of attack.

The good news for England is that, as they progress, teams will, most likely, look to attack them, leaving space for their speed and physicality to exploit. But the squad lack guile and magic, completely unnecessarily, and it’s not clear Tuchel really groks that.

Anderson, Rice and Bellingham are all fantastic players, but none have the deftness around the box to play quick combinations, or the eye to thread through little passes. It was obvious at half-time that, given what was available, the wise move was to hook one of the first two for Kobbie Mainoo, who is brilliant at finding space in traffic.

Or, in other words, a balanced midfield is not three power-players; at least one touch-player is required, and Mainoo is the only one England have. Perhaps you might say Eberechi Eze is that too, and he came on far too late to influence the game or for it to look like the coaching staff are on top of the problem.

I agree with Barney here: this was a small-space game, in which England used big-space players.

Partly this is because of the squad Thomas Tuchel picked. If I was facing England and you offered me Noni Madueke, Cole Palmer and Phil Foden, I know which of those three I’d back myself against. Madueke is a decent player, but no more than that; he isn’t special, and the other two are.

Palmer, in particular, has the ability to change the pace of a game and do surprising things others can’t, exactly what you need against an organised low block. But that wast the only glaring issue: Lewis Hall would’ve given England natural width on the left and also excellent passing out of defence, but he’s not even in the squad; and, though Trent Alexander-Arnold is no one’s idea of a proper defender, if you’re using him it’s because you need a goal, and leaving his delivery and craft at home makes absolutely no sense.

I wonder if these errors reflect a manager unfamiliar with tournament football; Tuchel has decided to play a particular way, and picked a collection of profiles he thinks can do that. But that’s left him without the means to change things properly; if things go wrong, he can swap players, but what if, as yesterday, the issue is the system and its principles?

And was Jordan Pickford fortunate not to get a red card when he hared out of box to collide with Abdul Fatawu?

I feel not. Had Fatawu got a touch on the ball, Pickford was toast, but because neither player did, I don’t think we can say there was a foul. Both went for it, both missed, so it makes most sense is to call it a collision.

I don’t really see how you can’t give it. Fatawu was in and Konsa launches into him, getting nowhere near the ball with no chance of getting at the ball – which makes it a red card too.

As far as goalless draws go, I thought it an engaging one. But plenty of things for Thomas Tuchel to ponder, which we’ll dig into into which we’ll dig presently.

This “I’m back” situation, though; it’ll take more than bagging a brace against Uzbekistan for that to be so.

Roberto Martínez has options, too. He could play a wide player up front – Pedro Neto has done it for Chelsea – or Goncalo Ramos, who’s a striker.

But it’s not just Ronaldo preventing this team from working as it should – Bernardo Silva was left out and, if they’re to fulfil their potential – they’ve got the players to win the thing – he must surely play a key role. I’d get him into a midfield three with Vitinha and João Neves, then have Bruno Fernandes and Neto with free roles behind – if we must – Ronaldo.

Surely no one rhose surname isn’t Dos Santos Aveiro really thinks that, though? Ronaldo can still finish – he’ll never lose that – but it’s very hard to even come up with rationale, never mind believe rationale, that says the best version of this Portugal team contains him.

We go again! We’ll begin by reflecting on the latest action – Portugal getting their competition going by thrashing Uzbekistan, England and Ghana near-enough securing passage to the knockouts, Croatia just about seeing off Panama, now eliminated, and Colombia forcing their way past DR Congo.

Then, when we’ve done that, we’ll build up to today’s action, featuring the final round of matches in Group B – Switzerland v Canada and Bosnia and Herzegovina v Qatar; Group C – Morocco v Haiti and Scotland v Brazil… and Group A – South Africa v South Korea and Czechia v México.

I reckon some people might have some thoughts about all of that lot, so we’ll share those of our writers, but do send in yours too.
